overview.summary: jsonwebtoken is Auth0's reference Node implementation of RFC 7519 JSON Web Tokens, published to npm as `jsonwebtoken` v9.0.3. It is a tiny, dependency-light library (three public functions — `sign`, `verify`, `decode` — plus three error classes) that wraps `jws` for the actual JWS signing/verification and layers on claim semantics (exp/nbf/aud/iss/sub/jti/nonce/maxAge), option schema validation, and a hard-won set of key-confusion defenses. What is distinctive is how much of the code is defensive rather than functional: roughly half of sign.js and verify.js is dedicated to coercing untrusted key material into `crypto.KeyObject`s, rejecting alg/key-type mismatches (the classic RS256→HS256 confusion attack), and enforcing a 2048-bit RSA modulus floor. It targets any Node service that issues or consumes JWTs, and ships both callback-async and synchronous-throwing modes of every entrypoint.

system_map.summary: This is a pure library with no server, no database, and no network I/O of its own — the only runtime boundary is the Node `crypto` module and the `jws` package. `index.js` is the whole public API surface: it re-exports `decode.js`, `verify.js`, `sign.js`, and the three error classes from `lib/`. Support modules in `lib/` are all single-purpose: feature-detection booleans gated on `process.version` via `semver`, a `ms`-backed timespan parser, and the asymmetric key/algorithm compatibility matrix. Build is nonexistent (plain CommonJS, no transpile); test is `mocha`, coverage is `nyc mocha --use_strict`, lint is `eslint .`. Deployment is npm publish driven by `semantic-release` in a two-workflow release dance on `master`.

claims.claim: `index.js` is the sole entrypoint and exports exactly six symbols: `decode`, `verify`, `sign`, `JsonWebTokenError`, `NotBeforeError`, `TokenExpiredError` — there is no class, no factory, no configuration object.

All cryptography is delegated to the `jws` package (`^4.0.1`): `jws.decode` in decode.js, `jws.sign`/`jws.createSign` in sign.js, and `jws.verify` in verify.js. This repo contains no hashing, HMAC, or signature code of its own.

The runtime dependency set is deliberately minimal and old-school: `jws`, `ms`, `semver`, and seven separately-published single-function lodash packages (`lodash.includes`, `lodash.isboolean`, `lodash.isinteger`, `lodash.isnumber`, `lodash.isplainobject`, `lodash.isstring`, `lodash.once`).

Node version capability is resolved at require-time, not call-time, by three boolean modules that `semver.satisfies(process.version, ...)`: `lib/psSupported.js` (`^6.12.0 || >=8.0.0`), `lib/asymmetricKeyDetailsSupported.js` (`>=15.7.0`), and `lib/rsaPssKeyDetailsSupported.js` (`>=16.9.0`).

PS256/PS384/PS512 are spliced into the algorithm allow-lists at module load only when `PS_SUPPORTED` — into `SUPPORTED_ALGS` at index 3 in sign.js, and appended to both `PUB_KEY_ALGS` and `RSA_KEY_ALGS` in verify.js.

The error hierarchy is hand-rolled ES5 prototype inheritance, not `class extends Error`: `JsonWebTokenError` calls `Error.call(this, message)` and manually sets `this.message`, and `NotBeforeError`/`TokenExpiredError` do `Object.create(JsonWebTokenError.prototype)` and add a `date`/`expiredAt` field.

`lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` owns the key-type↔algorithm compatibility matrix (`allowedAlgorithmsForKeys` for `ec`/`rsa`/`rsa-pss`) and the ES-curve mapping (`allowedCurves`: ES256→prime256v1, ES384→secp384r1, ES512→secp521r1). It is the single shared gate called by both sign and verify.

`lib/timespan.js` is the only time-arithmetic module; it converts a `ms`-parseable string or a raw number into an absolute epoch-seconds timestamp, and returns `undefined` (not an error) for unparseable input, pushing error construction onto its three callers.

Developer commands are `npm test` (bare `mocha`), `npm run coverage` (`nyc mocha --use_strict`), `npm run lint` (`eslint .`), and `npm run update-changelog` (`conventional-changelog -p conventionalcommits -i CHANGELOG.md`). `npm run prepare` installs husky hooks.

CI is five GitHub Actions workflows: `test.yml` (PR-triggered matrix over Node 16/18/20/22/24), `commitlint.yml` (PR-triggered conventional-commit validation), `prepare-release.yml` and `release.yml` (both on push to master, mutually exclusive via a `chore(release):` head-commit-message guard), and `sca-scan.yml` (Snyk, via a pinned reusable workflow from `auth0/devsecops-tooling`).

Publishing is `semantic-release` configured in `.releaserc.json` on the `master` branch, with conventional-commits analysis, npm publish from repo root, a `prepareCmd` of `git diff --exit-code`, and a `verifyReleaseCmd` that runs a ReversingLabs `rl-wrapper` scan over the `npm pack` tarball before release.

The published npm tarball is narrowed by the `files` allow-list to `lib`, `decode.js`, `sign.js`, `verify.js` — tests, `bin/`, and workflows never ship. `.npmignore` additionally excludes `opslevel.yml`.

feature_catalog.summary: The user-facing surface is three functions, each with a dual sync/async calling convention selected by whether a trailing callback is supplied. `sign` turns a payload plus key into a compact JWS, mapping option names onto registered claim names and computing time-based claims. `verify` is the security-critical path: it re-decodes, resolves a key (possibly via an async key-lookup callback for JWKS/kid workflows), enforces an algorithm allow-list, checks key/alg compatibility, verifies the signature, then runs seven independent claim checks. `decode` is the deliberately unauthenticated escape hatch. Twelve signing algorithms plus `none` are supported, and a set of explicit backwards-compatibility escape valves (`allowInsecureKeySizes`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`) let callers opt out of the newer hardening.

claims.claim: `jwt.sign(payload, secretOrPrivateKey, [options, callback])` supports thirteen options validated by `sign_options_schema`: `expiresIn`, `notBefore`, `audience`, `algorithm`, `header`, `encoding`, `issuer`, `subject`, `jwtid`, `noTimestamp`, `keyid`, `mutatePayload`, `allowInsecureKeySizes`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` — and rejects any key not in that schema with `"<key>" is not allowed in "options"`.

Four sign options are sugar that write registered claims, via the `options_to_payload` table: `audience`→`aud`, `issuer`→`iss`, `subject`→`sub`, `jwtid`→`jti`. Supplying both the option and the raw claim is an error (`Bad "options.<x>" option. The payload already has an "<claim>" property.`).

Non-object payloads (strings, numbers, Buffers) are supported for signing but reject the seven object-only options listed in `options_for_objects` with `invalid <opts> option for <typeof> payload`; a Buffer payload round-trips as its string form.
`mutatePayload: false` (the default) shallow-clones the payload with `Object.assign({}, payload)` before adding `iat`/`exp`/`nbf`, which is what makes signing a frozen or sealed payload work.
`options.encoding` (default `utf8`) is passed through to `jws`, so `{encoding: 'binary'}` produces a differently-encoded payload segment for non-ASCII characters.

`jwt.verify(token, secretOrPublicKey, [options, callback])` supports thirteen options: `algorithms`, `audience`, `complete`, `issuer`, `jwtid`, `ignoreExpiration`, `ignoreNotBefore`, `subject`, `clockTolerance`, `maxAge`, `clockTimestamp`, `nonce`, `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`.

`secretOrPublicKey` may be a key-lookup function `(header, cb)` — the JWKS/`kid` integration point — but only when a callback is also supplied; otherwise verify fails with `verify must be called asynchronous if secret or public key is provided as a callback`.
Audience matching accepts a string, a `RegExp`, or an array of either, and matches if ANY token `aud` entry matches ANY expected audience — an any-to-any `some`/`some` cross product.

`clockTolerance` (seconds of slack) and `clockTimestamp` (override for "now") apply to `nbf`, `exp`, and `maxAge` uniformly; `clockTimestamp` must be a number or verify fails early with `clockTimestamp must be a number`.

`maxAge` is an independent expiry ceiling computed from `payload.iat`, requires a numeric `iat` (`iat required when maxAge is specified`), and cannot loosen `exp` — a token past `exp` still fails even with `maxAge: '1000y'`.
`complete: true` on either `verify` or `decode` returns `{header, payload, signature}` instead of the bare payload — this is how callers reach `kid` and `alg` for key selection.
`jwt.decode(token, options)` performs no signature verification at all, and silently swallows a `JSON.parse` failure on the payload — returning the raw string payload rather than throwing.

data_flow.summary: There are exactly two input boundaries — the caller-supplied `(payload | jwtString, key, options)` tuple — and one output boundary, either a returned/thrown value or a `(err, result)` callback invocation. No state is owned across calls: the library is entirely stateless, with the only module-level mutable structures being the algorithm allow-list arrays built at require time. The central transform on both paths is key normalization: whatever the caller passes (string, Buffer, PEM, JWK-ish object) is funnelled through `crypto.createPrivateKey`/`createPublicKey` with a `createSecretKey` fallback into a `KeyObject`, and every downstream decision reads `key.type`, `key.asymmetricKeyType`, and `key.asymmetricKeyDetails` off that normalized object. Claim data flows one way on sign (options → payload properties → JWS) and one way on verify (JWS → decoded payload → claim assertions → returned payload).

claims.claim: On sign, key material normalization is a try/catch cascade: if not already a `KeyObject`, attempt `createPrivateKey(secretOrPrivateKey)`, fall back to `createSecretKey(Buffer.from(...))` for strings, and on double failure emit `secretOrPrivateKey is not valid key material`.

Verify mirrors that cascade with `createPublicKey` then `createSecretKey`, producing `secretOrPublicKey is not valid key material` — this is what converts a hostile object with a throwing `toString` into a clean error instead of arbitrary execution.

The JWS header is assembled by `Object.assign` with a fixed precedence: computed `{alg, typ, kid}` first (alg defaults to `HS256`, `typ` is `'JWT'` only for object payloads, `kid` comes from `options.keyid`), then `options.header` spread last so it can override any of them including `alg`.

A single `timestamp` value — `payload.iat || Math.floor(Date.now()/1000)` — is computed once and is the base for both `nbf` and `exp`, guaranteeing the three time claims are internally consistent within one sign call.

On verify, the token is parsed twice: once shallowly as `jwtString.split('.')` for arity (`jwt malformed` when length !== 3) and signature-presence checks on `parts[2]`, and once fully through `decode(jwtString, {complete: true})`.

`options` is defensively shallow-cloned on entry to verify (`Object.assign({}, options)`) specifically because the function later writes `options.algorithms` when the caller omitted it — caller-supplied objects are never mutated.

When `options.algorithms` is absent, the allow-list is derived from the normalized key: `secret`→HS_ALGS, `rsa`/`rsa-pss`→RSA_KEY_ALGS, `ec`→EC_KEY_ALGS, everything else→PUB_KEY_ALGS. This binds the accepted alg set to the key material, not to the token.

The token-supplied `header.alg` flows into `jws.verify(jwtString, decodedToken.header.alg, secretOrPublicKey)`, but only after passing the allow-list membership check and the key-type compatibility check — the ordering at lines 144→152→165 is the whole defense.

The verified `payload` object returned to the caller is the same object produced by `decode`, not a copy — all seven claim checks read from it without transforming it, so callers receive attacker-influenced data verbatim (the README explicitly warns to sanitize it).

Both functions funnel every error through a single sink — `failure(err)` in sign and `done(err, data)` in verify — which dispatches to `callback(err)` when async or `throw err` when sync, so sync and async modes are guaranteed to produce identical errors.

`decode` normalizes the payload channel: `jws.decode` may return a string payload, which `decode` opportunistically `JSON.parse`s and keeps only if the result is a non-null object — otherwise the string passes through unchanged.

`timespan(time, iat)` is the shared conversion from relative to absolute time on both paths: it feeds `payload.nbf`/`payload.exp` on sign and `maxAgeTimestamp` on verify, using `ms()` for strings and plain addition for numbers.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows matter: module load (feature detection), signing, and verification. Module load is unusual in that it bakes Node-version capability into module-scope constants, so the same code path behaves differently on Node 14 vs Node 16 without any runtime branch. Signing is a long linear gauntlet of eleven guards before any crypto happens. Verification is the inverse-ordered gauntlet, and its ordering is load-bearing: algorithm allow-listing and key-type checks must both precede `jws.verify`. Both entry functions branch at the very end into callback vs synchronous return.

claims.claim: MODULE LOAD: `require('jsonwebtoken')` → index.js requires decode/verify/sign → sign.js requires `lib/psSupported` → `semver.satisfies(process.version, '^6.12.0 || >=8.0.0')` → if true, `SUPPORTED_ALGS.splice(3, 0, 'PS256','PS384','PS512')` executes at module scope. Algorithm support is therefore frozen at first require.

SIGN step 1-2: normalize arity (`typeof options === 'function'` → shift to callback), compute `isObjectPayload` as `typeof payload === 'object' && !Buffer.isBuffer(payload)`, then build `header` via `Object.assign`.
SIGN step 3-4: reject missing key unless `algorithm === 'none'`, then coerce to `KeyObject` via `createPrivateKey` → `createSecretKey` fallback.

SIGN step 5: enforce symmetry — `header.alg.startsWith('HS')` requires `key.type === 'secret'`; `/^(?:RS|PS|ES)/` requires `key.type === 'private'`; and for non-ES RSA algs, `asymmetricKeyDetails.modulusLength < 2048` is rejected (guarded by an `!== undefined` check for pre-Node-15 where the field is absent).

SIGN step 6-8: `validatePayload` (allowUnknown=true, checks only iat/exp/nbf are numbers) → clone payload unless `mutatePayload` → reject `exp`+`expiresIn` and `nbf`+`notBefore` double-specification → `validateOptions` (allowUnknown=false).

SIGN step 9-11: `validateAsymmetricKey(header.alg, key)` unless opted out → compute `timestamp` and apply `noTimestamp`/`iat` → `timespan` for `nbf` and `exp` → copy the four `options_to_payload` claims.

SIGN terminal branch (async): wrap callback in `once()`, then `jws.createSign({header, privateKey, payload, encoding})` with `.once('error', callback)` and `.once('done', ...)`; the done handler re-checks `signature.length < 256` as a pre-Node-15 proxy for the 2048-bit modulus rule.

SIGN terminal branch (sync): `jws.sign({header, payload, secret, encoding})` returns the token, followed by the identical `signature.length < 256` check which `throw`s rather than calling back. Both branches carry a `TODO: Remove ... once node 15+ is the minimum supported version`.

VERIFY step 1-4: arity normalization → clone options → build `done` (callback or throw-on-error closure) → validate `clockTimestamp`/`nonce`/`allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` shapes → compute `clockTimestamp` → reject falsy or non-string `jwtString` → split into exactly 3 parts.

VERIFY step 5-6: `decode(jwtString, {complete: true})` inside a try/catch (returns `invalid token` if falsy), then choose `getSecret` — either the caller's key-lookup function or a trivial wrapper that immediately yields the static key. All remaining logic runs inside that callback.

VERIFY step 7: the three-way signature/key presence matrix — signature-without-key → `secret or public key must be provided`; key-without-signature → `jwt signature is required`; neither-plus-no-algorithms → `please specify "none" in "algorithms"`.

VERIFY step 8-10 (the security core, in this exact order): coerce key → derive default `algorithms` from key type → reject `header.alg` not in the list (`invalid algorithm`) → reject HS-alg-with-non-secret-key and RS/PS/ES-alg-with-non-public-key → `validateAsymmetricKey` → only then `jws.verify`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is the strongest part of the repo: ~258 `it()` blocks across 30 mocha files in `test/`, backed by chai assertions, sinon fake timers, and 17 checked-in PEM fixtures covering RSA, RSA-PSS, EC (three curves), DSA, and deliberately-invalid keys. The signature move is `test/test-utils.js`, which runs every sign/verify twice — once sync, once async — under a frozen clock and asserts the two produce byte-identical tokens or deep-equal errors; this is why the sync/async parity invariant actually holds. Coverage is configured with hard nyc thresholds, but the CI workflow runs bare `mocha`, so those thresholds and eslint are never enforced on PRs. Test naming is split between a per-claim convention (`claim-*.test.js`, `option-*.test.js`) and older topic/regression files (`*.tests.js`, `issue_*.tests.js`).

claims.claim: The framework stack is mocha 5 + chai 4 + sinon 6, with `atob` used to independently decode base64url segments in encoding tests. There is no `.mocharc`, so mocha's default `./test/*.js` glob picks up every file in `test/`.

`test/test-utils.js` exports `signJWTHelper` and `verifyJWTHelper`, both of which freeze time with `sinon.useFakeTimers({now: Date.now()})`, run the sync call in a try/catch, then run the async call and assert equality of token or error before restoring the clock.

`expectEqualError` exists because chai does not deep-equal errors (the helper cites chaijs/chai#1009); it compares `message` and `name` explicitly plus every enumerable property, which is how `expiredAt`/`date` payloads on the error subclasses get verified.

Option/claim validation is tested exhaustively by table-driven loops over ~15 bad values (`true, false, null, -1.1, Infinity, NaN, ' ', '', [], ['foo'], {}, {foo:'bar'}` …), applied per-claim in `claim-exp.test.js`, `header-kid.test.js`, and siblings.
`test/claim-aud.test.js` is the largest test file at 436 lines and 36 `it()` blocks, reflecting that audience matching (string/regex/array cross-product) is the most branch-heavy claim check.

`test/jwt.asymmetric_signing.tests.js` is parameterized: it builds an `algorithms` map of RS256/ES256 (plus PS256 when `PS_SUPPORTED`) each with `pub_key`, `priv_key`, and an `invalid_pub_key` that is deliberately not the pair of `priv_key`, then runs the same describe block per algorithm.
Security regressions are explicitly locked in by `test/jwt.malicious.tests.js`: HMAC-with-RSA-key confusion (both KeyObject and PEM form) and the malicious-`toString` Buffer-impersonation RCE vector.

Historical bugs are pinned by dedicated regression files: `issue_70.tests.js` (PEM headers), `issue_147.tests.js` (signing an `Object.seal`ed payload), `issue_304.tests.js`, and `rsa-public-key.tests.js`.

`test/validateAsymmetricKey.tests.js` unit-tests the key-matrix module directly (not through sign/verify), including the no-key and no-algorithm short-circuit paths and the PS/curve branches gated on the feature-detection booleans.
nyc is configured with `check-coverage: true` and thresholds of 95% lines, 95% statements, 100% functions, 95% branches, excluding `./test/**` — a genuinely strict bar.

GAP: `test.yml` runs only `npm test` (bare mocha). Neither `npm run coverage` nor `npm run lint` appears in any workflow, so the nyc thresholds and the eslint ruleset are advisory only and can silently regress.

A known-broken case is parked rather than fixed: `it.skip('should work with none algorithm where secret is falsy')` in async_sign, annotated with a link to node-jws issue #62 — the async `alg: none` path with a falsy secret is untested and known not to work.

risk_map.summary: As a library whose entire job is security, nearly every line in verify.js is a security-sensitive path, and the ordering of its checks is the load-bearing invariant — any reordering that lets `jws.verify` run before the algorithm allow-list check reintroduces the classic JWT confusion attacks. The most concrete correctness defect is in sign.js's `options_to_payload` loop, where `return failure(...)` inside a `forEach` callback does not abort the enclosing function, so in async mode the callback can fire twice. Secondary risks cluster around Node-version-conditional code that CI does not fully exercise, deliberately silent error swallowing in `decode`, a very old eslint pinned at v4, and release workflows that handle several third-party secrets. Blast radius for any change here is unusually wide: this package sits in the dependency tree of a large fraction of Node auth stacks.

claims.claim: CORRECTNESS BUG: in the `options_to_payload` loop, `return failure(...)` only returns from the `forEach` arrow — the outer sign function continues. In async mode `failure` invokes the raw callback with an error at line 221, and since `callback` is not yet wrapped by `once()` (that happens at line 230), signing proceeds and the callback is invoked a second time with a valid token.

SECURITY-CRITICAL ORDERING: the allow-list check (`options.algorithms.indexOf(header.alg) === -1`), the key-type symmetry check, and `validateAsymmetricKey` all sit between `decode` and `jws.verify`. Any edit that moves `jws.verify` earlier, or that trusts `header.alg` before line 144, reopens the RS256→HS256 confusion class.

`options.header` is `Object.assign`ed LAST when building the sign header, so a caller passing `{header: {alg: 'none'}}` silently overrides `options.algorithm` — and the downstream key/alg checks then run against the overridden value. This is by design but is a sharp edge for callers who build headers from user input.

`decode` swallows all `JSON.parse` errors in an empty `catch (e) { }`, returning the raw string payload instead. Callers that assume an object back from `decode` will see a string on malformed tokens with no signal.

The `signature.length < 256` heuristic is an acknowledged stopgap for the 2048-bit modulus rule on Node < 15, duplicated in both the sync and async branches with matching `TODO: Remove ...` comments — a two-site invariant that can drift.

No source file uses `'use strict'`, so sloppy-mode semantics apply — e.g. `delete payload.iat` on a primitive string payload under `noTimestamp` is a silent no-op rather than a TypeError. Notably `npm run coverage` runs mocha with `--use_strict` while `npm test` does not, so the two commands exercise different semantics.

The EC curve check dereferences `key.asymmetricKeyDetails.namedCurve` without a null guard; it is protected only by the module-load `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` semver boolean, and that whole block is excluded from coverage by `istanbul ignore next`.

The verified payload returned by `verify` is the same object `decode` produced, unsanitized and fully attacker-controlled in content; the README carries an explicit warning to treat it as user input, which implies downstream misuse is a known recurring problem.

`allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes: true` disables `validateAsymmetricKey` on both sign and verify, and a test asserts it lets an ES256-labelled token be processed with an RSA key — a documented footgun kept only for backwards compatibility.

`release.yml` handles six secrets (`PRODSEC_TOOLS_ARN`, `PRODSEC_TOOLS_USER`, `PRODSEC_TOOLS_TOKEN`, `RLSECURE_LICENSE`, `RLSECURE_SITE_KEY`, `SIGNAL_HANDLER_TOKEN`) and embeds credentials in a pip `--index-url`. Mitigations are in place — `persist-credentials: false`, `mask-aws-account-id: true`, SHA-pinned actions — but this job is the highest-value supply-chain target in the repo.

`prepare-release.yml` parses the next version out of semantic-release's human-readable stdout with `awk '/The next release version is/{print $NF}'` — a brittle coupling to log wording that would silently produce an empty version if the message text changes.

DEAD CODE: `bin/changelog` is a standalone conventional-changelog script with hardcoded `releaseCount: 19` and a commented-out `preset: 'jshint'`, but nothing references it — `package.json` and `prepare-release.yml` both go through the `update-changelog` npm script instead (per commit b924272).

extension_points.summary: This library has no plugin system by design — a JWT implementation with third-party extension hooks would be a security liability. What it does have are a handful of declarative tables that are the intended edit sites for new capability, and one genuine runtime hook. The tables are the two option schemas and the `options_to_payload` map in sign.js, the four algorithm arrays in verify.js, and the `allowedAlgorithmsForKeys`/`allowedCurves` matrices in `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` — adding an algorithm means touching all three files coherently. The one caller-facing hook is verify's function-valued `secretOrPublicKey`, which is where JWKS clients plug in. Feature detection for new Node capabilities follows a one-file-per-boolean convention in `lib/`.

claims.claim: PRIMARY RUNTIME HOOK: `secretOrPublicKey` as a `(header, secretCallback)` function is the documented integration point for JWKS/`kid`-based key resolution; internally the static-key case is normalized into the same shape so there is exactly one code path after line 101.

Adding a new sign option means one entry in `sign_options_schema` with an `isValid` predicate and a `message` — the generic `validate(schema, allowUnknown, object, parameterName)` walker requires no other change, and unknown options are rejected because `validateOptions` passes `allowUnknown: false`.

`registered_claims_schema` is the parallel table for payload claims and is validated with `allowUnknown: true`, so arbitrary custom claims pass through while `iat`/`exp`/`nbf` are type-enforced — this asymmetry is the extension point for application-specific claims.

`options_to_payload` is a two-column map from option name to claim name; adding a new registered-claim shortcut is a one-line addition there, and the conflict-detection and copy logic applies automatically.

`options_for_objects` is the companion list declaring which options are meaningless for non-object payloads; any new object-only option must be added here too or it will be silently accepted on a string payload.

Algorithm support is defined in four arrays: `SUPPORTED_ALGS` (sign.js) and `PUB_KEY_ALGS` / `EC_KEY_ALGS` / `RSA_KEY_ALGS` / `HS_ALGS` (verify.js). A new algorithm requires edits in both files plus `allowedAlgorithmsForKeys`.

`allowedAlgorithmsForKeys` maps `asymmetricKeyType` → permitted `alg` values and is the single authority on key/algorithm pairing; an unrecognized key type throws `Unknown key type "<type>"`, so new key types must be registered here or they are rejected outright.
`allowedCurves` maps ES algorithms to required named curves and is the place to add a curve; it is consulted only under `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED`.

New Node-version feature gates follow a one-module-per-flag convention: a three-line file exporting `semver.satisfies(process.version, '<range>')`, consumed as a module-scope constant. Three such files already exist.

New error types extend the hierarchy by the ES5 pattern in `lib/NotBeforeError.js`: call `JsonWebTokenError.call(this, message)`, set `this.name`, add the payload field, then `prototype = Object.create(JsonWebTokenError.prototype)` and restore `constructor`. New types must also be re-exported from `index.js` to be reachable.

New verify-time claim checks slot into the linear block between `jws.verify` and the return, following the established `if (options.X) { if (payload.y !== options.X) return done(new JsonWebTokenError(...)) }` shape used by issuer/subject/jwtid/nonce.

Test convention for new options/claims: add a `test/option-<name>.test.js` or `test/claim-<name>.test.js` file that uses `testUtils.signJWTHelper`/`verifyJWTHelper` plus `asyncCheck`, so sync/async parity is enforced for free.

agent_handoff.summary: Treat this as a security library first and a JavaScript project second: the check ordering in verify.js and the guard cascade in sign.js are the product, and reordering them is never a safe refactor even when it looks like cleanup. Style is intentionally conservative CommonJS ES5/ES6 with no build step, no TypeScript, no async/await, and no strict mode — match it rather than modernize it. Read the four root JS files and `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js` before touching anything; they are under 600 lines combined. Commits must be Conventional Commits because commitlint gates PRs via husky locally and a workflow in CI, and because semantic-release derives the version from them.

claims.claim: READ FIRST, in order: `index.js`, `sign.js`, `verify.js`, `decode.js`, `lib/validateAsymmetricKey.js`. That is the entire library — under 600 lines total — and everything else in `lib/` is a three-line helper.

RUN: `npm test` for the fast loop (mocha over `test/`), `npm run coverage` before proposing a merge (nyc enforces 95/95/100/95 and will fail the command), and `npm run lint` manually since no workflow runs it.

COMMIT FORMAT: Conventional Commits are mandatory. `.husky/commit-msg` runs `npx --no -- commitlint --edit $1` locally and `commitlint.yml` re-validates every commit in a PR range; `@commitlint/config-conventional` is the ruleset.

STYLE: 2-space indent enforced by both `.editorconfig` and the eslint `indent` rule; no semicolon rule, no quote rule. eslint is pinned at v4 with `ecmaVersion: 6`, so avoid syntax newer than ES2015 in new code paths or the lint run will fail to parse.

TRAP — check ordering: in verify.js, lines 144 (allow-list), 148-152 (key-type symmetry), and 154-160 (key/alg matrix) must all remain before line 165 (`jws.verify`). Moving or short-circuiting any of them is a vulnerability, not a refactor.

TRAP — dual calling convention: every change to sign or verify must work identically in sync (throws) and async (callback) mode. `test/test-utils.js` asserts byte-equality of tokens and deep-equality of errors across the two, so a one-sided fix will fail loudly.

TRAP — `return` inside `forEach`: the existing `options_to_payload` loop already has this bug (a `return failure(...)` that does not abort the function). Do not copy that pattern into new claim-copy logic, and be aware that fixing it changes observable async callback behavior.

TRAP — Node-conditional code: three `semver.satisfies` booleans are evaluated at module load. Code behind `ASYMMETRIC_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` and `RSA_PSS_KEY_DETAILS_SUPPORTED` will not execute on your local Node unless it is new enough, and is excluded from coverage — verify such changes against the CI matrix (16/18/20/22/24), not just locally.

SAFE EDIT BOUNDARY: adding a claim check, a validated option, or a test is low-risk and well-patterned. Changing key coercion (`createPrivateKey`/`createPublicKey`/`createSecretKey` cascades), the algorithm arrays, or `validateAsymmetricKey` is high-risk and touches published security behavior.

DO NOT EDIT casually: `CHANGELOG.md` is generated by `npm run update-changelog` during the prepare-release workflow, and `package.json` `version` is bumped by `npm version --no-git-tag-version` in that same workflow. Hand-editing either will conflict with the release automation.

RELEASE SHAPE: pushing to master triggers `prepare-release.yml`, which opens a `release/vX.Y.Z` PR titled `chore(release): X.Y.Z`; merging that PR matches the `startsWith(..., 'chore(release):')` guard and triggers `release.yml` to run `npx semantic-release`. The two workflows are mutually exclusive by that guard.

New public API or option changes must be reflected in `README.md`, which is the only user documentation and is structured as `jwt.sign` / `jwt.verify` / `jwt.decode` / Errors & Codes / Algorithms supported.

overview.summary: This is the lodash monorepo root: the hand-maintained single-file UMD source `lodash.js` (v4.18.1, ~546 KB, one IIFE wrapping a `runInContext` factory), the `fp/` converter that re-wraps every method into immutable auto-curried iteratee-first data-last form, and a small Node build/doc toolchain under `lib/` that copies, minifies, webpacks, and doc-generates artifacts into `dist/` and `doc/`. It is not an application — it is a library plus its release machinery, consumed by downstream repos (`lodash-cli`, the `npm` branch) that call `build:main-modules`/`build:fp-modules` with a target directory. What's distinctive is the test posture: ~1750 QUnit assertions in a single 814 KB `test/test.js` that deliberately sabotages host globals ("bizarro" shims), plus vendored Backbone and Underscore suites run against lodash, driven in Node and across six Playwright browser projects. The repo is now under OpenJS Foundation governance with a published threat model that explicitly scopes prototype pollution and `_.template` code injection as in-scope vulnerability classes.

system_map.summary: There is no server or CLI entrypoint; the shipped artifact is `lodash.js`, declared as `main` in a `private: true` package.json, exported via a three-way UMD tail (AMD `define`, CommonJS `freeModule.exports`, global `root._`). All build logic lives in `lib/`, split into `lib/common/` (file copy, uglify wrapper, error-throwing callback, Hash), `lib/main/` (dist, modules, docdown, site HTML) and `lib/fp/` (webpack dist, `.jst`-templated module emission, FP wiki). The only persistent storage is the filesystem: `dist/` for builds and `doc/README.md` for generated API docs. Eight GitHub Actions workflows cover Node 4–25, four Bun versions, browser matrix, docs generation, dist-sync verification, CodeQL, OSSF Scorecard and Renovate. Deployment is out-of-repo — the Release Team publishes to npm, and `dist/lodash.core.js` is produced by the external `lodash-cli`, not by `npm run build`.

claims.claim: The package is `private: true` with `main: "lodash.js"` and `engines.node >= 4.0.0`, so the repo itself is never published; it is the source-of-truth checkout that other release tooling consumes.

`lodash.js` is a single `;(function() { ... }.call(this))` IIFE whose entire API is built inside a `runInContext(context)` factory at line 1449; the module-level `var _ = runInContext()` at line 17232 creates the default instance.

The export tail branches three ways in strict order — AMD `define.amd` (also assigning `root._` to survive script-tag loading), then `freeModule.exports` for Node/CommonJS, then a bare global assignment — which is why the file works unchanged in every listed CI runtime.

Runtime-boundary detection is done once at the top level via `freeGlobal`/`freeSelf`/`Function('return this')()` for `root`, plus `freeExports`, `freeModule`, `moduleExports` and `freeProcess` for Node-only features like `Buffer` and `util.types`.

`npm run build` is only `build:main && build:fp`: `lib/main/build-dist.js` copies `lodash.js` → `dist/lodash.js` and minifies it, while `lib/fp/build-dist.js` runs two webpack passes (`fp/_mapping.js` → `dist/mapping.fp.js`, `fp/_convertBrowser.js` → `dist/lodash.fp.js`, both UMD) then minifies.

Minification is centralized in `lib/common/minify.js`, which shells into `uglify-js@2.7.5` with `unsafe: true`, `pure_getters: true`, `ascii_only: true` and a `/@license/` comment filter from `lib/common/uglify.options.js`.

All build scripts share the same async shape: `lib/common/file.js` returns `_.partial`-applied `fs.copy`/`minify`/`fs.writeFile` thunks that are handed to `async.series` with `util.pitch` as the terminal callback, and `pitch` simply rethrows any error.

`lib/common/mapping.js` wraps `fp/_mapping.js` in a null-prototype `Hash` (recursively, via `_.transform` with `Hash.prototype = Object.create(null)`), so build-time lookups like `mapping.skipFixed[name]` can't collide with inherited `Object.prototype` keys.

Documentation is a two-stage pipeline: `lib/main/build-doc.js` runs `docdown` over `lodash.js` in either `github` or `site` style and writes `doc/README.md`; `lib/main/build-site.js` then feeds that markdown through `marky-markdown` + `cheerio` and emits `doc/<version>.html` with Jekyll front matter.
`doc/README.md` is a checked-in 295 KB generated artifact (its first line carries the `v4.18.1` docdown title), and `doc/*.html` is gitignored — so the markdown is versioned but the site HTML is not.

Eight workflows exist: `ci-node.yml` (Node 4 through 25 on ubuntu, `npm run validate`), `ci-bun.yml` (Bun 1.0–1.3), `browser-testing.yml` (Playwright), `ci-docs.yml`, `ci-dist-sync.yml`, `codeql.yml`, `scorecards.yml`, `renovate.yml`.

Every third-party action is SHA-pinned (e.g. `actions/checkout@3d3c42e5...` v7.0.1, `github/codeql-action/init@b96794f0...` v4.38.0), and Renovate is self-hosted monthly with `minimumReleaseAge: 14d` and npm major updates disabled.

feature_catalog.summary: User-facing surface is the lodash API itself (~300 methods attached to the `lodash` function plus a lazy-evaluating chain wrapper), the `fp` variant, and the four per-method build/doc npm scripts. `fp/_mapping.js` is the declarative feature table that defines the entire FP surface: aliases, arity buckets, rearg orders, spread configs, mutation classes and skip lists. The repo also ships two interactive HTML surfaces — a QUnit test runner with build/loader dropdowns, and a Benchmark.js perf page comparing lodash against Underscore. There is no HTTP API, no routes, and no CLI subcommands; the `lib/*/build-*.js` scripts are the closest thing to commands and take their target directory from the last `process.argv` element.

claims.claim: The full lodash API is assembled by explicit `lodash.<name> = <fn>` assignment inside `runInContext`, including `lodash.runInContext`, `lodash.VERSION` and the chainable `lodash.prototype.*` sequence methods (`at`, `chain`, `commit`, `next`, `plant`, `reverse`, `toJSON`/`valueOf`/`value`).

Lazy evaluation is a first-class feature: `LazyWrapper.prototype.clone/reverse/value` are installed and a `realNames` registry maps minified function names back to method names so shortcut fusion survives minification.

`fp/_mapping.js` declares the FP surface across 12 exported tables — `aliasToReal`, `aryMethod`, `aryRearg`, `iterateeAry`, `iterateeRearg`, `methodRearg`, `methodSpread`, `mutate`, `realToAlias`, `remap`, `skipFixed`, `skipRearg`.

The FP immutability guarantee is table-driven: `mapping.mutate` classifies mutating methods into `array` (fill, pull*, remove, reverse), `object` (assign*, defaults*, merge*) and `set` (set, setWith, unset, update, updateWith), each wrapped with a different cloner.

`fp/_convertBrowser.js` self-installs when loaded after lodash in a browser: if a global `_` with `runInContext` exists, it reassigns `_ = browserConvert(_.runInContext())`, converting the page's lodash in place.

FP conversion is configurable per-call and per-method through five boolean options — `cap`, `curry`, `fixed`, `immutable`, `rearg` — each defaulting to `true`, exposed as `fp.convert({...})` and `fp.someMethod.convert({...})`.

`npm run build:main-modules <target>` copies `dist/lodash.core.js`, `dist/lodash.core.min.js` and `dist/lodash.min.js` into a target directory as `core.js`, `core.min.js` and `lodash.min.js` — the per-method npm package layout.

`npm run build:fp-modules <target>` globs the target's existing `*.js` modules (ignoring `_*.js`, `core.js`, `fp.js`, `index.js`, `lodash.js`), adds alias and remap paths, and emits one `fp/<name>.js` per method chosen from four `.jst` templates (`alias`, `category`, `thru`, `module`).

`npm run doc:fp` renders the public FP-Guide wiki page from `lib/fp/template/doc/wiki.jst`, computing the method lists at build time with helpers `toFuncList` (sorted, chunked by 5) and `toArgOrder` (index permutation → `(a, b, c)` string).

The QUnit runner page exposes a build selector (lodash dev/prod, lodash-core dev/prod) and a loader selector (none, Curl, Dojo, RequireJS) that rewrite `location.href` query params, letting a human test any build/loader combination in-browser.

`perf/index.html` plus `perf/perf.js` is a Benchmark.js A/B suite that loads lodash and a comparison library (default Underscore), scores each into `score.a`/`score.b`, and renders output through an embedded Firebug Lite console.
`test/remove.js` is a small standalone Node utility that takes a `/pattern/flags` string plus a file path and strips matched line groups in place — used to prune generated sources.

data_flow.summary: Two distinct flows exist. At library runtime, data enters as plain JS values through method arguments, is normalized by `castPath`/`toKey`/`baseIteratee`, mutated or cloned by `base*` internals, and exits either as a new value or — in chain mode — as a `LazyWrapper`/`lodash` wrapper holding `__wrapped__` and an `__actions__` queue that is only drained on `.value()`. At build time, the input boundary is `lodash.js` plus `fp/_mapping.js`; transforms are `fs.copy`, `uglify.minify`, `webpack`, `docdown` and `_.template`-compiled `.jst` files; the output boundary is the filesystem (`dist/`, `doc/`, or an arbitrary `target` from `process.argv`). The FP path is unusual: `_mapping.js` is pure data that is read three times — by `_baseConvert` at runtime, by `build-modules.js` to decide which template to emit, and by `build-doc.js` to render the wiki.

claims.claim: Property paths are the main untrusted input boundary: `castPath` converts strings/arrays to key arrays and `toKey` normalizes each segment before any read or write in `baseGet`/`baseSet`/`baseUnset`.

Writes funnel through `assignValue` → `baseAssignValue`, which special-cases the key `__proto__` by using `Object.defineProperty` with an own data descriptor rather than plain assignment, so it lands on the object instead of the prototype.
Deep merge reads go through `safeGet`, which returns `undefined` for `__proto__` and for `constructor` when it resolves to a function — cutting the read side of the pollution chain.

Chain state lives on the wrapper instance: `mixin` installs prototype methods that clone `__actions__` via `copyArray`, push `{func, args, thisArg}`, carry `__chain__` forward, and defer execution until `.value()`.

In `_baseConvert`, each method flows through a fixed transform pipeline — immutability wrapper → `castFixed` (arity cap or `flatSpread`) → `castRearg` (argument permutation) → `castCap` (iteratee arity cap) → `castCurry` — with `methodSpread[name].afterRearg` deciding whether fixed or rearg runs first.

The FP converter owns two state sources: a `pristine = func.runInContext()` snapshot used so `.convert()` re-derives from unconverted methods, and a `defaultHolder` placeholder that is stamped onto both the wrapped and original function as `.placeholder`.

Conversion output is assembled as `pairs` of `[name, wrappedFn]` — first for every name in `mapping.aryMethod[1..4]`, then for remaining own function keys — and only then assigned back onto `_`, deliberately leaving `_.prototype` untouched so chaining still works.
`_.set`-family immutability in FP is achieved by `cloneByPath`, which walks the resolved path cloning each level but skipping values that are functions, errors or WeakMaps.

Build data flows from `fp/_mapping.js` → `lib/common/mapping.js` (null-prototype Hash) → `lib/fp/build-modules.js`, where `_.union(mapping.aryMethod[1..4])` forms `aryMethods` and drives the `isThru` decision for every emitted module.

`.jst` templates are compiled to functions at require time by `file.globTemplate`, which globs `*.jst`, keys them by basename, and runs each through `_.template` — so `template.module`, `template.alias`, `template.wiki` are lodash templates executed with `{name, mapping}` data.

The doc HTML flow mutates markdown through five ordered regex rewrites (uncommenting docdown HTML hints, converting `[source]`/`[npm package]` links after `<h3>`) before Cheerio DOM passes `autoLink`, `renameLodashId`, `removeHorizontalRules`, `removeMarkyAttributes`, `repairMarkyHeaders`, `tidyHighlights`.

The site build derives its output filename from the document itself — it removes the first `<h1>`, reads the version out of its `<span>`, and writes `doc/<version>.html`; if that span is missing the front matter records `version: null`.

behavior_traces.summary: Four flows matter here: library initialization, an FP conversion, the `npm test` path, and the browser-test path. Library init is entirely synchronous at require time. The Node test path is unusual because `pretest` forces a full build first, meaning `npm test` cannot run without webpack and uglify succeeding. The browser path is a three-stage `document.write` cascade that deliberately corrupts globals before loading lodash, snapshots the result as `lodashBizarro`, restores the globals, then loads the real build and the suite.

claims.claim: Library startup: the outer IIFE defines constants and regexes → detects `freeGlobal`/`root`/`freeModule` → defines `runInContext` → calls `var _ = runInContext()` at line 17232 → picks one of three export branches. No async work and no I/O occurs.

Inside `runInContext`, the sequence is: default the context from `contextProps` → alias built-ins (`Array`, `Object`, `Function`, …) → derive `maskSrcKey` from `context['__core-js_shared__']` → build `reIsNative` from `funcToString.call(hasOwnProperty)` → define all internals → attach them to `lodash` → return `lodash`.

FP conversion of the whole library: `baseConvert(util, name, func, options)` detects `isObj`/`isLib` → builds `config` from the five option flags → snapshots `pristine` → iterates `mapping.aryMethod[1..4]` calling `wrap(key, func, _)` for each → sweeps remaining own function keys attaching only `.convert` → assigns all pairs onto `_` → sets `_.convert` and `_.placeholder` → finally assigns aliases.

A single method's wrap: `wrap()` resolves `realName` via `aliasToReal` → applies a named special-case wrapper if one exists in `wrappers` (castArray, iteratee, mixin, nthArg, rearg, runInContext) → else applies `wrapImmutable` with the cloner chosen from `mapping.mutate` → then runs the castFixed/castRearg/castCap/castCurry chain → attaches `.convert` and `.placeholder`.

`npm test` fires `pretest` → `npm run build` → `build:main` (copy + minify) → `build:fp` (webpack mapping, webpack fp, minify) → then `test:main` = `node test/test` and `test:fp` = `node test/test-fp`.

`node test/test` bootstrap: resolve `filePath` from argv (defaulting to `../lodash.js`, then `fs.realpathSync` + `require.resolve`) → build the `ui` object with `isModularize`/`isStrict` flags → poison `global.root` with a throwing getter → require `qunit-extras` → load the previous stable lodash from `node_modules/lodash/lodash.js` as `lodashStable` → `interopRequire(filePath)` as `_`.

`test.js` then reaches into internals for coverage: it derives `Hash`, `MapCache`, `ListCache` and `Stack` constructors by inspecting `_.memoize.Cache.__data__.hash.constructor` and by capturing the stack argument passed to an `_.isMatchWith` customizer.

At the end of both Node suites the same tail runs: set `QUnit.config.asyncRetries = 10` and `hidepassed = true`, and when `document` is absent set `noglobals = true` then `QUnit.load(); QUnit.start();`.

`test-fp.js` startup differs: it builds a `convert` shim that dispatches to either `root.fp` (browser, pre-built `dist/lodash.fp.js`) or `require('../fp/_baseConvert.js')` (Node), then produces `fp` either by `_.noConflict()` juggling or by `convert(_.runInContext())`.

Browser test startup, stage 1: `test/index.html` loads stable lodash + QUnit + qunit-extras + platform + `test-ui.js`, calls `addBizarroMethods()` to null out `Object.create`, `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols`, `Symbol`, `Promise`, `Set`, `WeakMap` and patch `Function.prototype.toString`, then `document.write`s `ui.buildPath`.

Stage 2 captures the sabotaged instance as `lodashBizarro`, clears `window._`, calls `removeBizarroMethods()` to restore every global, then `document.write`s either the build + `test.js` directly or the selected AMD loader.

Stage 3 (AMD path) configures the loader with three package aliases pointing at the same files through different paths — `lodash`, `shimmed` (`./abc/../`) and `underscore` (`./xyz/../`) — loads all three, tags each with `moduleName`, optionally pulls `_baseEach`/`_isIndex`/`_isIterateeCall`, then `require(['test'])` and `QUnit.start()`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is QUnit 2 (`qunitjs` + `qunit-extras`) driven two ways: directly under Node via `node test/test` and `node test/test-fp`, and in browsers via Playwright asserting `0 failed` on four static pages. Coverage of the main library is very broad — 307 QUnit modules and ~1754 assertions in `test/test.js` alone, plus 85/134 for FP — and is supplemented by running the vendored Backbone and Underscore suites against lodash. Style is enforced by JSCS across `lodash.js`, `fp/`, `lib/`, `perf/` and `test/`, and docs are tested by executing every README code fence via `markdown-doctest`. The notable gaps are the `lib/` build scripts themselves and the Playwright runner's coarse assertion.

claims.claim: `test/test.js` contains 307 `QUnit.module(` and 1754 `QUnit.test(` calls in a single 814 KB file; `test/test-fp.js` adds 85 modules and 134 tests.
`npm run validate` is the CI gate everywhere — it chains `npm run style` (four JSCS invocations) and `npm test` — and is what both `ci-node.yml` and `ci-bun.yml` run.
The Node matrix is exhaustive and non-fail-fast: Node 4 through 25 on ubuntu-latest, with a special step installing `npm@3.10.10` for Node 5 because of npm 3 package-format bugs.

Bun CI needs a workaround before it can install: it runs `npm i --lockfile-version 3 --package-lock-only` first because the committed `package-lock.json` is an older lockfile version, flagged with a TODO.

Browser coverage runs six Playwright projects (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, Microsoft Edge via msedge channel, Mobile Safari/iPhone 12, Mobile Chrome/Pixel 5) with `retries: 2` under CI and a 120s per-test timeout chosen to exceed the 60s in-page wait.

Each Playwright spec asserts only that the literal text `0 failed` becomes visible — it does not read which tests ran, so a page that silently fails to load its suite and renders nothing will time out rather than report a specific failure.

Cross-library regression coverage: `test/backbone.html` runs Backbone's own 7 test files against lodash after `mixin`-ing 17 lodash methods and aliasing `indexBy`→`keyBy`, `invoke`→`invokeMap`, `rest`→`tail`.

`test/underscore.html` runs Underscore's 7 suites against lodash and carries a large `QUnit.config.excused` map enumerating known, accepted behavioral divergences (e.g. `chunk` size 0, `difference` OO-style, `drop` alias).

The suite tests lodash against a deliberately hostile environment: `addBizarroMethods` removes `Object.create`/`Symbol`/`getOwnPropertySymbols`, stubs `Promise`/`Set`/`WeakMap` with `noop`, makes `Map` return a plain object on first construction, and fakes `WinRTError` plus `global`/`exports`/`module`.
There is an explicit minification guard test asserting no exported method name is ≤2 characters except `_`, `at`, `eq`, `gt`, `lt` — catching accidentally shipped minified production builds.

Documentation is executable: `npm run test:doc` runs `markdown-doctest doc/*.md` with a setup file that deletes `global['__core-js_shared__']` and injects the real `_` plus `lodash-doc-globals` into every example's scope.

JSCS enforces ~40 rules including `requireEarlyReturn`, `disallowKeywords: ["with"]`, `validateQuoteMarks: '`, 2-space indentation and JSDoc type/param/return checks, but with `maxErrors: 2000` so a large backlog can exist without failing.

risk_map.summary: The security-sensitive surface is narrow but sharp: `_.template` compiles to a real `Function`, and the path-write family (`_.set`, `_.unset`, `_.merge`, `_.defaultsDeep`) has layered prototype-pollution guards that are the subject of prior CVEs. The repo's own `threat-model.md` scopes these precisely. Structurally, the largest risk is coupling: `lodash.js` is 546 KB in one file that every contributor edits, `test/test.js` is 814 KB, and `fp/_mapping.js` is a hand-maintained table that must stay in lockstep with the method list or the FP build silently drifts. `dist/lodash.core.js` is not produced by `npm run build`, so the dist-sync workflow cannot detect a stale core build. CI also pulls two unpinned packages from the network at test time.

claims.claim: `_.template` builds a source string and evaluates it with `Function(importsKeys, sourceURL + 'return ' + source)`; the project's own threat model calls it insecure, cites CVE-2021-23337, and states it will be removed in v5.

`_.template`'s hardening is two regex checks: `sourceURL` has all whitespace collapsed to spaces so a newline can't escape the `//#` comment, and `variable` is rejected if it matches `/[()=,{}\[\]\/\s]/`.
`baseSet` returns the object untouched if any path segment is `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype` — a blanket block that also silently no-ops legitimate writes to a literal `constructor` key.

`baseUnset` uses a different, narrower rule than `baseSet`: it blocks `__proto__` only when the object lacks an own `__proto__`, and blocks `constructor`/`prototype` only in non-terminal positions — the asymmetry is deliberate but easy to break when editing one and not the other.

Prototype-pollution defense is spread across four unrelated call sites — `baseAssignValue`, `baseSet`, `baseUnset`, `safeGet` — plus `isKey`'s `value !== '__proto__'` check, so a new path-writing method added without touching all of them would be unprotected.

`dist/lodash.core.js` carries the header `Build: lodash --source ./lodash.js core -o ./dist/lodash.core.js` and is produced by the external `lodash-cli`; `npm run build` only regenerates `lodash.js`, `lodash.min.js`, `lodash.fp.js` and `mapping.fp.js`.

Because `npm run build` never writes `dist/lodash.core*.js`, `ci-dist-sync.yml`'s `git diff --exit-code dist/` will pass even when the core build is stale relative to an edited `lodash.js` — a silent staleness hole in the sync gate.

`browser-testing.yml` installs two packages that are not in `package.json` and are unpinned: `npm install -D @playwright/test@latest` and `npx http-server`, both fetched from the registry on every CI run despite every GitHub Action being SHA-pinned.

`npm run doc:fp` invokes `node lib/fp/build-doc` with no target argument, so `_.last(process.argv)` resolves to the script's own path and `fs.writeFile(target, ...)` writes the wiki output next to the build script rather than to an intended doc location.

The build toolchain is pinned to end-of-life tooling: `uglify-js` exactly `2.7.5`, `webpack ^1.14.0` (using the webpack-1-only `OccurenceOrderPlugin` and `DedupePlugin`), `jscs ^3.0.7` and `istanbul 0.4.5`, while Renovate is configured to never propose major npm updates.

The test suite deletes and replaces host globals (`Object.create`, `Symbol`, `Map`, `Promise`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `Function.prototype.toString`) and restores them by hand in a separate function — an asymmetry that leaks global state into all subsequent tests if `removeBizarroMethods` drifts from `addBizarroMethods`.

`test/test.js` intentionally defines a non-configurable throwing getter on `global.root` and calls `require('vm').runInNewContext` to build a cross-realm fixture — both are process-level side effects that make the suite hostile to running inside other harnesses.

extension_points.summary: The intended way to add a method is: implement it in `lodash.js`, attach it with `lodash.<name> = <name>` in the assignment block, add tests in `test/test.js`, and — if it should exist in FP form — register it in the right `fp/_mapping.js` tables. `fp/_mapping.js` is the real registry: arity bucket, rearg order, iteratee cap, spread config, mutation class, alias and remap are all declarative. `_baseConvert`'s `wrappers` object is the escape hatch for methods whose conversion can't be expressed in tables. At runtime, `_.mixin` and `_.runInContext` are the library's public extension APIs, and `templateSettings` is the configuration hook for `_.template`.

claims.claim: The method registry is the literal assignment block near the end of `runInContext` — every public method appears as `lodash.<name> = <name>`, and omitting a line there makes an implemented function unreachable.

`mapping.aryMethod[1|2|3|4]` is the primary FP registration point: `_baseConvert` iterates exactly these buckets to decide which methods get wrapped, and `lib/fp/build-modules.js` unions them into `aryMethods` to decide `module.jst` vs `thru.jst`.

`_baseConvert`'s `wrappers` object is a named override table — `castArray`, `iteratee`, `mixin`, `nthArg`, `rearg`, `runInContext` each get bespoke conversion logic that bypasses the table-driven pipeline.

`mapping.remap` lets an FP-only method name map onto a different real lodash method, and `build-modules.js` reads it both to emit extra module paths and, via `_.get(mapping.remap, name, name)`, to write the correct `require` inside the generated module.
`mapping.aliasToReal` drives three things at once: alias resolution inside `wrap()`, the `alias.jst` re-export module, and the generated FP-Guide's alias listing.
Opting a method out of FP transforms is declarative: add its name to `mapping.skipFixed` (no arity cap) or `mapping.skipRearg` (no argument reordering), both read inside `castFixed`/`castRearg`.

The `lib/fp/template/modules/*.jst` set is the emission plugin surface — `getTemplate()` dispatches to `alias`, `category`, `thru` or `module` based on `isAlias`/`isCategory`/`isThru`, so a new module shape means a new `.jst` plus a branch there.

`file.globTemplate` auto-discovers templates by glob and keys them by basename, so dropping a new `.jst` into `lib/fp/template/modules/` makes it available as `template.<basename>` without registering it anywhere.

`_.mixin(object, source, options)` is the public plugin API: it walks `baseFunctions(source)`, assigns each onto the target, and when the target is a function also installs a chain-aware prototype method honoring `options.chain`.

`_.runInContext(context)` is the sandboxing extension point — the `contextProps` array enumerates the 30 substitutable globals, documented with the example of swapping `setTimeout` for `setImmediate`.
`lodash.templateSettings` is the documented configuration object for `_.template`'s `escape`/`evaluate`/`interpolate` delimiters, `imports` and `variable`, read at the top of `template()`.

The doc pipeline is configured by the `config` object in `lib/main/build-doc.js`, keyed `base`/`github`/`site` and merged with `_.defaults`; adding a third output style means adding a key there and a matching npm script.

agent_handoff.summary: Read `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md` first — it states the core rule that for additions or bug fixes you should only modify `lodash.js` and add tests in `test/`, and explicitly says not to regenerate `dist/` or `doc/`. That rule is in tension with `ci-dist-sync.yml`, which fails the build if `npm run build` changes `dist/`, so a change to `lodash.js` does require a rebuild and commit of `dist/lodash.js` and `dist/lodash.min.js`. The style gate is JSCS with unusual rules (`requireEarlyReturn`, no `with`, single quotes, 2-space indent, JSDoc types required), so match the surrounding code exactly. Never hand-edit `dist/*`, `doc/README.md`, or anything under `vendor/` — they are generated or vendored.

claims.claim: CONTRIBUTING states the contract directly: "For additions or bug fixes you should only need to modify `lodash.js`. Include updated unit tests in the `test` directory... Don't worry about regenerating the `dist/` or `doc/` files."

Despite that guidance, `ci-dist-sync.yml` runs `npm run build` then `git diff --exit-code dist/` and fails with an explicit "Run 'npm run build' and commit the updated dist/ files" error — so an agent editing `lodash.js` must also commit the rebuilt `dist/lodash.js` and `dist/lodash.min.js`.
`dist/lodash.js` is currently byte-identical to `lodash.js` (the build is a plain `fs.copy`), so any `lodash.js` edit produces a mechanically predictable dist diff.

Files an agent must read before editing, in order: `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md`, `package.json` scripts, `lodash.js` (the target region plus the `lodash.<name> =` assignment block), `fp/_mapping.js` if the change touches FP, and `threat-model.md` if the change touches `set`/`merge`/`unset`/`template`.

Tests to run locally: `npm test` (which force-builds via `pretest`), or the faster direct `node test/test` and `node test/test-fp` once a build exists; `npm run validate` is the full gate that CI uses.
`node test/test <path>` accepts an alternate build path as its last argument, defaulting to `../lodash.js` — this is how you point the suite at `dist/lodash.min.js` or a core build.

The Node suite requires the previous published lodash to be installed at `node_modules/lodash/lodash.js` as `lodashStable`; if it's missing the suite prints "The stable lodash dev dependency should be at least a version behind master branch" and silently returns without running.

Style must match JSCS: two-space indent, single quotes (double only to avoid escaping), semicolons required, `with` banned, early returns required, and JSDoc blocks needing types, param descriptions and return types.
Naming conventions are prescribed: prefer `index`, `array`, `iteratee` over `i`, `arr`, `fn`; JSCS additionally enforces `requireCamelCaseOrUpperCaseIdentifiers`.
An optional pre-push hook is available by creating a root `.opt-in` file containing `pre-push`, which runs `npm run validate` on push.

Safe edit boundary — do not touch: `dist/*` (generated, and `lodash.core*` only by external lodash-cli), `doc/README.md` (docdown output), `vendor/**` (Backbone/Underscore/json2/firebug-lite), `package-lock.json` unless deliberately updating deps.

Trap: adding an FP-visible method means touching `fp/_mapping.js` in up to five places (`aryMethod` bucket, plus any of `aliasToReal`, `remap`, `methodRearg`, `iterateeAry`, `mutate`, `skipFixed`, `skipRearg`) or the FP build and wiki will silently omit or mis-wrap it.

commit.subject: v16.4.0-canary.38

health.summary: Deterministic scan scored 96 source files across simple size, churn, structural, test-adjacency, and performance-risk signals. 24 hotspots surfaced; average score is 7.1/10. Treat these as review leads, not proof of a bug.

history.subject: v16.4.0-canary.38

Enable AI upgrade for canary (#99001)
fix(turbo-persistence): preserve write errors on writer drop (#98840)
