overview.summary: This is the facebook/react monorepo at commit 59aff3e — the React runtime (isomorphic `react`, the Fiber reconciler, the Fizz SSR server, the Flight/Server-Components client+server, DevTools, and the Scheduler) plus a largely independent `compiler/` sub-project holding the React Compiler in both TypeScript (`babel-plugin-react-compiler`) and an in-progress Rust port (12 `react_compiler_*` crates behind a napi bridge). It is a library-publishing repo, not an app: nearly every artifact is a Rollup-built npm bundle produced per *release channel* (stable / canary / experimental / www-classic / www-modern / xplat), with behaviour toggled by ~67 `enable*` feature flags that are fork-substituted at build time. What is distinctive is the fork/shim architecture — `ReactFiberConfig`, `ReactFeatureFlags`, `ReactFlightServerConfig` and friends are placeholder modules that *throw* unless Rollup or Jest swaps in a renderer-specific implementation — and a CI matrix that runs the same Jest suite 18 ways × 5 shards to prove every channel behaves.

system_map.summary: There is no single entrypoint; the repo is a set of publishable packages under `packages/` (workspace glob in `package.json`) plus a nested Yarn/Cargo workspace under `compiler/`. The public runtime entrypoints are `packages/react/index.js` (isomorphic), `packages/react-dom/client.js` → `ReactDOMRoot.createRoot`, `packages/react-dom/server.node.js` → Fizz, and `packages/react-server-dom-*/server.*` → Flight. Everything is compiled by `scripts/rollup/build.js`, driven by a bundle table in `scripts/rollup/bundles.js` and a module-substitution table in `scripts/rollup/forks.js`; `build-all-release-channels.js` runs the whole thing once per channel and rewrites versions from `ReactVersions.js`. There is no database or persistent storage layer — the only 'storage' is the Fiber tree in memory, npm as the deployment target, and GitHub Actions artifacts. Tests never run `jest` directly; `scripts/jest/jest-cli.js` picks one of six configs and spawns Jest with channel/env/variant globals injected.

claims.claim: `package.json` declares a Yarn-1 workspace over `packages/*` with `packageManager: yarn@1.22.22`, and blocks direct Jest invocation via `"jest": {"testRegex": "/scripts/jest/dont-run-jest-directly\\.js$"}` — all testing must go through `yarn test` → `scripts/jest/jest-cli.js`.

`ReactVersions.js` is the single source of truth for publishing: `ReactVersion = '19.3.0'`, a `stablePackages` map (react-reconciler 0.34.0, scheduler 0.28.0, react-refresh 0.19.0, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1) and `experimentalPackages = ['react-markup']`; a package not listed there is never published.

The client entrypoint is `createRoot(container, options)` in `packages/react-dom/src/client/ReactDOMRoot.js`, which calls `createContainer(..., ConcurrentRoot, ...)`, `markContainerAsRoot`, then `listenToAllSupportedEvents(rootContainerElement)` before returning a `ReactDOMRoot` wrapper whose `.render` delegates to `updateContainer`.

The reconciler's public surface is `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberReconciler.js` — `createContainer`, `updateContainer`, `updateContainerSync`, and `updateContainerImpl` which builds an update via `createUpdate(lane)` / `enqueueUpdate` and hands off to `scheduleUpdateOnFiber(root, rootFiber, lane)`.

The renderer boundary is the `ReactFiberConfig` shim: `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberConfig.js` contains only `throw new Error('This module must be shimmed by a specific renderer.')` — Rollup (`scripts/rollup/forks.js`) and Jest (`scripts/jest/setupHostConfigs.js`) both substitute a real host config per renderer.

`scripts/shared/inlinedHostConfigs.js` enumerates ~20 renderer targets by `shortName` (`dom-browser`, `dom-node`, `dom-edge-webpack`, `dom-node-turbopack`, `dom-node-parcel`, `dom-bun`, `fabric`, `markup`, `dom-fb`, …), each with an `entryPoints` list — this table is the authoritative list of runtime boundaries.

Cooperative scheduling lives in `packages/scheduler/src/forks/Scheduler.js`: `unstable_scheduleCallback` pushes into a min-heap, `workLoop` drains it, and `shouldYieldToHost` yields once `timeElapsed >= frameInterval` (default `frameYieldMs`, tunable via an fps setter); the host callback is scheduled via `setImmediate` when available, else `MessageChannel` (chosen to dodge the 4 ms `setTimeout` clamp), else `setTimeout`.

Builds are orchestrated by `scripts/rollup/build.js` (`buildEverything` → `createBundle` per bundle × bundleType, with Babel, Google Closure Compiler for prod bundles, and `rollup-plugin-prettier` for FB/dev output) over the ~20 `bundleTypes` declared in `scripts/rollup/bundles.js` (NODE_DEV/PROD/PROFILING, ESM_*, BUN_*, FB_WWW_*, RN_OSS_*, RN_FB_*, BROWSER_SCRIPT, CJS_DTS/ESM_DTS).

`scripts/rollup/build-all-release-channels.js` shells out to the build once per channel via `spawnSync`, then `processStable(buildDir)` / `processExperimental(buildDir)` rewrite package versions using the short SHA from `git rev-parse HEAD`, merging the experimental tree into the stable one.

The compiler is a second workspace: `compiler/Cargo.toml` defines a Rust workspace over `crates/*` plus `packages/babel-plugin-react-compiler-rust/native`, pinned to edition 2024 / rust-version 1.85, version `0.0.1-oidc.0`, with a `[profile.release]` of fat LTO + 1 codegen unit + strip (documented as shrinking the shipped `index.node` from 11.2 MB to 7.2 MB).

The Rust compiler is reached from JS through napi: `native/src/lib.rs` exposes `#[napi] pub fn compile(ast_json, scope_json, options_json) -> String`, spawning a dedicated 64 MB-stack thread and catching panics; `src/bridge.ts` loads it with `require('../native')` and passes JSON.

External integrations are narrow and mostly tooling-side: npm registry (`scripts/release/publish.js`, `scripts/release/ci-npmrc`), Discord webhooks in four notify workflows, Vercel for the compiler playground (`compiler/apps/playground/vercel.json`), and Algolia's `beta-react` index queried by the React MCP server.

feature_catalog.summary: User-facing surface is API surface, not screens. `packages/react/src/ReactClient.js` is the canonical export list for the isomorphic package; `react-dom` fans out to client, server (Node/Edge/Browser/Bun), static prerender and test-utils entrypoints; `react-server-dom-{webpack,turbopack,parcel,esm,unbundled,fb}` each ship a bundler-specific Flight client+server pair. Tooling packages are first-class features too: `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` (now also re-exporting compiler-derived rules), `react-refresh` (Fast Refresh Babel plugin + runtime), DevTools in five packaging flavours, and two MCP servers. Behaviour is further gated by ~67 `enable*` flags in `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js`, inspectable via `yarn flags`.

claims.claim: The isomorphic `react` package exports the full modern surface including `use`, `cache`, `cacheSignal`, `Activity`, `ViewTransition`, `addTransitionType`, `unstable_SuspenseList`, `unstable_TracingMarker`, and `__COMPILER_RUNTIME` — enumerated in `packages/react/index.js` and implemented in `ReactClient.js`.

Hooks are exported from `packages/react/src/ReactHooks.js` and include the newer `useOptimistic`, `useActionState`, `useEffectEvent`, `useSyncExternalStore`, `useDeferredValue`, `useCacheRefresh` and `use`.

`react-dom` ships eleven distinct entrypoints — `client.js`, `server.js`/`server.node.js`/`server.edge.js`/`server.browser.js`/`server.bun.js`, `static.js`/`static.node.js`/`static.edge.js`/`static.browser.js`, `profiling.js`, `test-utils.js`, `unstable_testing.js` and `unstable_server-external-runtime.js`.

Streaming SSR is `renderToPipeableStream` in `packages/react-dom/src/server/ReactDOMFizzServerNode.js`, which builds a request via `createRequestImpl` → `createRequest`, kicks off `startWork(request)`, and exposes `pipe(destination)` that calls `startFlowing(request, destination)`.

Server Actions are a shipped feature: `decodeAction(body, serverManifest)` scans FormData for `$ACTION_REF_*` / `$ACTION_ID_*` keys, resolves the reference through `loadServerReference`, and returns the action pre-bound to the remaining FormData; `decodeFormState` handles `$ACTION_KEY` for `useActionState`.

Flight (RSC) supports multiple request body shapes on the server: `decodeReply`, `decodeReplyFromBusboy` (multipart uploads) and `decodeReplyFromAsyncIterable`, all exported from `ReactFlightDOMServerNode.js`.

Taint APIs `taintUniqueValue` and `taintObjectReference` guard against leaking server secrets to the client, backed by `TaintRegistryObjects` (WeakMap), `TaintRegistryValues` (refcounted Map) and a `FinalizationRegistry` cleanup hook; gated by `enableTaint = __EXPERIMENTAL__`.

`eslint-plugin-react-hooks` v7 ships `rules-of-hooks` and `exhaustive-deps` plus a set of compiler-derived rules merged in from `shared/ReactCompiler`, with `recommended` and `recommendedLatest` flat-config presets and a deprecated-rule shim for `component-hook-factories`.
Fast Refresh is two artifacts: `ReactFreshBabelPlugin.js` (build-time instrumentation) and `ReactFreshRuntime.js` (runtime registry / signature checking), published as `react-refresh@0.19.0`.

DevTools ships in five packaging flavours — `react-devtools` (standalone), `-core`, `-extensions` (browser extension), `-inline`, `-fusebox` (React Native / Chrome DevTools frontend) — all sharing `react-devtools-shared`, plus `react-devtools-shell` for local development.
`react-devtools-cdt-mcp` is a browser library that registers React inspection and profiling tools with `chrome-devtools-mcp`, published from its own workflow.

A second MCP server lives in the compiler: `compiler/packages/react-mcp-server` registers tools including `query-react-dev-docs` (Algolia-backed react.dev search) and a runtime-performance tool driven by headless Puppeteer.

data_flow.summary: On the client, input enters through DOM events (delegated at the root by `listenToAllSupportedEvents`) or imperative `root.render`, both of which funnel into `scheduleUpdateOnFiber(root, fiber, lane)`. State lives on the Fiber tree hanging off `FiberRoot`; the `lane` bitmask on `ReactFiberLane.js` is the priority currency that decides whether work is flushed synchronously, in a microtask, or via a Scheduler task. Output boundaries are the host config (`ReactFiberConfig`, substituted per renderer) and, for SSR/RSC, the stream `Destination` in Fizz/Flight. Cross-module state is deliberately routed through a single mutable singleton, `ReactSharedInternals` (`.H` = current hooks dispatcher, `.T` = current transition, `.A` = async dispatcher), which is itself a forked module so client and server get different instances.

claims.claim: All client updates converge on `scheduleUpdateOnFiber`, which marks the root (`markRootUpdated(root, lane)`), merges interleaved/render-phase lanes, and calls `ensureRootIsScheduled(root)`; sync updates on legacy roots additionally trigger `flushSyncWorkOnLegacyRootsOnly()` immediately.

`ensureRootIsScheduled` does not schedule work directly — it appends the root to an intrusive linked list (`firstScheduledRoot`/`lastScheduledRoot` via `root.next`), sets `mightHavePendingSyncWork = true`, and defers to a microtask that runs `processRootScheduleInMicrotask` → `scheduleTaskForRootDuringMicrotask`.

Priority is encoded as a 31-bit lane bitmask (`TotalLanes = 31`) with named lanes `SyncLane`, `InputContinuousLane`, `DefaultLane`, transition lanes, retry lanes, `IdleLane`, `OffscreenLane` and `DeferredLane`; `requestUpdateLane(fiber)` picks the lane for each update.

`performWorkOnRoot` decides between `renderRootConcurrent` and `renderRootSync` from `shouldTimeSlice`, which is false for blocking lanes, expired lanes, or `forceSync` — but forced true when `checkIfRootIsPrerendering(root, lanes)` so prerendering never blocks the main thread.

External-store consistency is re-validated after a concurrent render: if `isRenderConsistentWithExternalStores(finishedWork)` fails, `performWorkOnRoot` discards the result and re-runs `renderRootSync(root, lanes, false)` to block further mutation.

Hook state is read and written through a swappable dispatcher on the shared-internals singleton: `renderWithHooks` assigns `ReactSharedInternals.H` to `HooksDispatcherOnMount` or `HooksDispatcherOnUpdate` (DEV variants included) and resets it to `ContextOnlyDispatcher` when the component finishes.

`root.render(children)` writes nothing directly — it calls `updateContainer(children, root, null, null)`, which becomes an update object on the host-root fiber's update queue via `createUpdate(lane)` + `enqueueUpdate(rootFiber, update, lane)`.

DOM events are the other input boundary and are delegated once per root: `createRoot` and `hydrateRoot` each call `listenToAllSupportedEvents(container)` from `react-dom-bindings/src/events/DOMPluginEventSystem`, so per-node listeners are not attached.

On the server, Fizz's data flow is request-scoped: `createRequest(...)` builds a `Request`, `startWork(request)` renders tasks (`retryTask`, `renderNode`, `renderNodeDestructive`), and `startFlowing(request, destination)` drains completed segments through `flushCompletedQueues` into the stream.

Server-Action input crosses a trust boundary as untyped `FormData`: `decodeAction` copies every non-`$ACTION_` field into a fresh `FormData`, decodes bound args by replaying them through `createResponse`/`getRoot` in `decodeBoundActionMetaData`, and binds the result — so client-supplied bytes drive `resolveServerReference(bundlerConfig, id)`.
`decodeBoundActionMetaData` accepts an `arraySizeLimit` parameter threaded into `createResponse`, indicating the Flight reply parser has an explicit bound on attacker-controlled array sizes.

DevTools data flows over a batched message bus: `Bridge` wraps a `Wall`, queues events and flushes them on a `BATCH_DURATION` timer, sending typed `BackendEvents` (`overrideProps`, `overrideHookState`, `overrideState`, `overrideContext`) from frontend to backend.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows are worth walking: (1) client startup/first paint, from `createRoot` through the microtask scheduler into render and commit; (2) the compile flow, where Babel hands a function to either the TS `Pipeline.ts` or the Rust `pipeline.rs`; (3) the release flow, where a commit becomes npm artifacts. The commit phase in particular is a fixed three-pass sequence with `root.current = finishedWork` as the atomic swap point between mutation and layout, and passive effects flushed later. Each trace below names the functions in call order with line anchors.

claims.claim: Startup trace: `createRoot(container, options)` → validate via `isValidContainer` → `createContainer(container, ConcurrentRoot, …, onUncaughtError, onCaughtError, onRecoverableError)` → `markContainerAsRoot(root.current, container)` → `listenToAllSupportedEvents(rootContainerElement)` → `new ReactDOMRoot(root)`.

First render trace: `root.render(children)` → `updateContainer` → `updateContainerImpl` → `requestUpdateLane(current)` → `createUpdate(lane)` → `enqueueUpdate(rootFiber, update, lane)` → `scheduleUpdateOnFiber(root, rootFiber, lane)`.

Scheduling trace: `scheduleUpdateOnFiber` → `markRootUpdated(root, lane)` → `ensureRootIsScheduled(root)` → `ensureScheduleIsScheduled()` → `scheduleImmediateRootScheduleTask()` → (microtask) `processRootScheduleInMicrotask` → `scheduleTaskForRootDuringMicrotask` → `Scheduler_scheduleCallback(priorityLevel, performWorkOnRootViaSchedulerTask)`.

Render trace: `performWorkOnRoot(root, lanes, forceSync)` computes `shouldTimeSlice`, dispatches to `renderRootConcurrent` (line 2779) or `renderRootSync` (line 2623), then loops on the `RootExitStatus` — handling `RootInProgress` (yield, `startYieldTimer`), store inconsistency (re-render sync), and `RootErrored` (`getLanesToRetrySynchronouslyOnError` → `recoverFromConcurrentError`).

Component render trace: for each function component the reconciler calls `renderWithHooks`, which installs the mount-or-update dispatcher on `ReactSharedInternals.H`, invokes the component, then restores `ContextOnlyDispatcher`; `bailoutHooks` is the memoized fast path.

Commit trace: `commitRoot` (line 3725) → `commitBeforeMutationEffects(root, finishedWork, lanes)` → `commitMutationEffects(root, finishedWork, lanes)` → `root.current = finishedWork` (the tree swap, line 4051) → `commitLayoutEffects(finishedWork, root, lanes)` → `flushSpawnedWork()`; passive effects run later via `flushPendingEffects` → `commitPassiveMountEffects`.

Yield trace: inside a Scheduler task, `workLoop(initialTime)` drains the min-heap and stops when `shouldYieldToHost()` returns true (elapsed ≥ `frameInterval`); the continuation is re-armed by `schedulePerformWorkUntilDeadline()` through `setImmediate`/`MessageChannel`/`setTimeout`.

SSR trace: `renderToPipeableStream(children, options)` → `createRequestImpl` → `createRequest(...)` → `startWork(request)` (line 6370) → tasks retried through `retryTask`/`renderNode` → consumer calls `pipe(destination)` → `startFlowing(request, destination)` (line 6464) → `flushCompletedQueues` (line 6175); `abort(request, reason)` is the cancellation path (line 6557).

Server Action trace: HTTP POST FormData → `decodeAction(body, serverManifest)` → detect `$ACTION_REF_*` or `$ACTION_ID_*` → `decodeBoundActionMetaData` (for bound args) → `loadServerReference` → `resolveServerReference(bundlerConfig, id)` → `preloadModule` → `requireModule` → `bindArgs(fn, args)` → returned action `fn.bind(null, formData)`.

TS compile trace: `compileFn` builds `Environment` from `findContextIdentifiers(func)`, then runs `lower(func, env)` → `PruneMaybeThrows` → `ValidateContextVariableLValues` → `MergeConsecutiveBlocks` → `SSA` → `EliminateRedundantPhi` → `ConstantPropagation` → `InferTypes` → `AnalyseFunctions` → `InferMutationAliasingEffects` → `DeadCodeElimination` → `InferMutationAliasingRanges` → `InferReactivePlaces` → `buildReactiveFunction` → `renameVariables`, logging each step through the `log(value)` callback.

Rust compile trace mirrors it: `compile_fn` → `react_compiler_lowering::lower` → `validate_context_variable_lvalues` → `validate_use_memo` → `enter_ssa` → `eliminate_redundant_phi` → `infer_types` → `analyse_functions` → `infer_mutation_aliasing_effects` → `infer_mutation_aliasing_ranges` → validations → `infer_reactive_places` → `infer_reactive_scope_variables` → scope alignment passes.

The compiler is fault-tolerant rather than fail-fast: passes call `env.recordError(diagnostic)`, validation passes are wrapped in `env.tryRecord(() => pass(hir))`, and errors are aggregated at the end via `env.hasErrors()` / `env.aggregateErrors()` — `CompilerError.invariant()` is the only category that always throws.

testing_signals.summary: Jest 30 is the runtime test framework, with 544 test files under `packages/**/__tests__`, and it is deliberately unusable directly — `package.json`'s `testRegex` points at `dont-run-jest-directly.js`, forcing everything through `scripts/jest/jest-cli.js`. That CLI selects one of six configs (source, source-www, source-xplat, source-persistent, build, build-devtools) and injects `__DEV__`, `__EXPERIMENTAL__` and `__VARIANT__` globals; individual tests opt in/out of behaviour with `// @gate <flag>` pragmas resolved by `scripts/jest/TestFlags.js`. The compiler uses a different harness entirely: `yarn snap` over ~1,543 fixture files with `.expect.md` snapshots, plus Playwright e2e for the playground and the flight fixture. CI runs the runtime suite as an 18-config × 5-shard matrix; the Rust port has its own workflow gating on `cargo check`, `cargo build`, two shell test scripts and `yarn snap --rust`.

claims.claim: Jest is pinned at `^30.4.1` (`jest`, `jest-cli`, `jest-environment-jsdom`, `babel-jest`) with `jest-silent-reporter` and `jest-snapshot-serializer-raw` for output control.
There are 544 test files under `packages/**/__tests__/**/*.js`, spread across the runtime, DevTools shared, scheduler and shared packages.

`scripts/jest/jest-cli.js` is the only supported entry: it exposes `--project {default,devtools}`, `--releaseChannel {experimental,stable,www-classic,www-modern,xplat}`, `--env`, `--prod`/`--dev`, `--variant`, `--build`, `--persistent`, `--ci`, `--reactVersion` and `--sourceMaps`, then spawns Jest with the matching config file.

Six Jest configs cover the test surfaces: `config.source.js`, `config.source-www.js`, `config.source-xplat.js`, `config.source-persistent.js`, `config.build.js` and `config.build-devtools.js` — so the same specs are exercised against source and against built bundles.

`@gate` pragmas let a test declare its preconditions; `scripts/jest/TestFlags.js` resolves them against `shared/ReactFeatureFlags` plus environment flags `__DEV__`, `build`, `experimental`, `stable`, `variant`, `persistent`, and the deliberate escape hatches `FIXME: false` / `TODO: false` for known-broken tests.

`scripts/jest/setupHostConfigs.js` rewires module resolution so each test file resolves `react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberConfig` to the right renderer's host config, iterating over `inlinedHostConfigs` — without it every reconciler test would hit the throwing shim.

`packages/internal-test-utils` supplies the shared test vocabulary — `internalAct.js`, `ReactInternalTestUtils.js`, `consoleMock.js`, `shouldIgnoreConsoleError.js`/`shouldIgnoreConsoleWarn.js`, and `simulateBrowserEventDispatch.js` — and is itself tested.

The runtime CI matrix in `runtime_build_and_test.yml` runs 18 parameter sets (stable/experimental/www-classic/www-modern/xplat × development/production × variant true/false, plus two persistent configs) crossed with 5 shards, i.e. 90 parallel `yarn test` jobs.
CI also gates on non-test checks as separate jobs: `flow` (sharded by discovered inline configs), `check_generated_fizz_runtime`, `flags`, and `test-linter` for `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`.
There is a dedicated fuzz workflow (`runtime_fuzz_tests.yml`) separate from the main suite, so fuzzing is not part of the per-PR signal.

The compiler's test corpus is fixture-driven: ~1,543 `.js` fixtures under `babel-plugin-react-compiler/src/__tests__/fixtures`, each paired with a `.expect.md`, run via `yarn snap` (`-p <pattern>`, `-d` debug, `-u` update) as documented in `compiler/CLAUDE.md`.

Fixture naming encodes expected failure modes: `error.todo-*.js` means an unsupported feature that correctly bails with a Todo error, `error.bug-*.js` means a known bug producing the wrong error — so some fixtures are assertions about known gaps, not passing behaviour.

risk_map.summary: The genuinely security-sensitive surface is small but sharp: Flight's Server Actions turn attacker-controlled FormData into a module lookup and function invocation, the taint registry is the only guard against serialising server secrets to the client and it is experimental-only, and the DevTools extension bridges page-world `postMessage` to privileged `chrome.runtime` ports while also running string-`eval` payloads through `chrome.devtools.inspectedWindow.eval`. Operationally the biggest fragility is the fork/shim system — `ReactFiberConfig` and `ReactFeatureFlags` resolve differently under Rollup, Jest and Flow, so a change that passes locally can break a channel nobody ran. `ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` at 5,683 lines with ~60 exported functions and module-level mutable state is the highest blast-radius file in the repo, and the Rust port is a live second implementation of the compiler that must stay snapshot-identical to the TypeScript one.

claims.claim: `loadServerReference` resolves a client-supplied string id straight into `resolveServerReference(bundlerConfig, id)` → `preloadModule` → `requireModule`; the only validation is `typeof id !== 'string'` (which silently returns `null as any`), so the security boundary rests entirely on the bundler-generated `serverManifest`.

`decodeAction` distinguishes action fields purely by string prefix (`$ACTION_REF_`, `$ACTION_ID_`, `$ACTION_`) on attacker-controlled FormData keys, and a mismatch falls through to `throw new Error('Cannot handle action key. This is a bug in React.')` — a user-reachable throw framed as an internal invariant.

The taint protection against leaking secrets to the client is gated off by default outside experimental builds (`export const enableTaint = __EXPERIMENTAL__`), and `taintUniqueValue` early-returns when the flag is false — stable consumers get no taint enforcement.

`TaintRegistryValues` is a plain `Map<string|bigint, TaintEntry>` with manual refcounting in `cleanup()`, relying on `FinalizationRegistry`; the code explicitly notes that if `FinalizationRegistry` is absent it 'assume[s] that objects live forever' — a correctness cliff on older runtimes.

The DevTools extension executes code as strings in the inspected page: `evalScripts.js` defines a `.code` variant for each of `checkIfReactPresentInInspectedWindow`, `reload`, `viewElementSource`, `viewAttributeSource` and the selection bridges, intended for `chrome.devtools.inspectedWindow.eval()`.

The extension's content scripts relay untrusted page-world messages into privileged extension ports: `prepareInjection.js` listens on `window.addEventListener('message', ...)` and `proxy.js` forwards across `chrome.runtime.connect(...)` / `chrome.runtime.onMessage` and back out via `window.postMessage` — a classic content-script trust boundary.

The DevTools bridge lets the frontend write arbitrary values into a live app — `overrideProps`, `overrideState`, `overrideHookState`, `overrideContext` are first-class bridge events — so anything that can speak the bridge protocol can mutate application state.
`__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__` is installed as a page global and documented in-source as 'a de facto public API', giving any script on the page a handle on every mounted renderer.

`ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` is 5,683 lines with roughly 60 exports and heavy module-level mutable state (`workInProgressRoot`, `workInProgressSuspendedReason`, `workInProgressRootExitStatus`, `executionContext`), making it the single highest blast-radius file — almost every reconciler behaviour change lands here.

The fork system is fragile by design: `scripts/rollup/forks.js` substitutes 13 module paths (shared internals, feature flags, fiber config, stream/fizz/flight configs, `EventListener`, `useSyncExternalStore`) and Jest substitutes them differently — so a module can resolve three ways (Rollup, Jest, Flow) and only CI exercises all of them.

There are 13 `ReactFeatureFlags` forks (`www`, `www-dynamic`, `native-fb`, `native-oss`, `test-renderer`, `eslint-plugin.www`, `readonly`, …); a flag added to the base file without updating every fork is a known failure mode, which is exactly why CI has a dedicated `flags` job and a `/flags` skill.

`scripts/release/ci-npmrc` writes `//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}` and three compiler prerelease workflows inject `NPM_TOKEN` from repository secrets — any workflow change that widens trigger conditions on those files widens publish access.

extension_points.summary: The repo's main extension mechanism is the host-config pattern: write a `ReactFiberConfig.<renderer>.js`, register the renderer in `scripts/shared/inlinedHostConfigs.js` and add a fork rule, and you get a new React renderer sharing the reconciler unchanged. Bundles are similarly table-driven — add an entry to `scripts/rollup/bundles.js` and a version to `ReactVersions.js` and the build/publish pipeline picks it up. Inside the compiler, the pass list in `Pipeline.ts` / `pipeline.rs` is the ordered registry, `HIR/Globals.ts` is where hook aliasing signatures are declared, and `Environment.ts` is where feature flags live. For tooling, the ESLint plugin merges rules from a `allRules` map, the MCP servers register tools with `server.tool(name, description, schema, handler)`, and Jest behaviour is extended via `@gate` flags declared in `TestFlags.js`.

claims.claim: New renderers plug in through the host-config shim: implement the interface, then register in `scripts/shared/inlinedHostConfigs.js` with a `shortName` and `entryPoints`, and add a substitution branch in `scripts/rollup/forks.js` for `./packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberConfig.js`.

`packages/react-noop-renderer` is the reference implementation of that extension point — a full renderer with `persistent.js`, `server.js`, `flight-client.js`, `flight-server.js` and `flight-modules.js` variants, used as the testbed for reconciler features.

New publishable packages plug into `ReactVersions.js`: the header states 'Packages will not be published unless they are added here', with `stablePackages` for versioned output and `experimentalPackages` for sha-only builds.

New build outputs plug into the `bundles.js` table via `bundleTypes` and `moduleTypes` (`ISOMORPHIC`, `RENDERER`, …); `scripts/rollup/build.js#shouldSkipBundle` then decides per bundle×type whether to emit.

`scripts/rollup/forks.js` is itself an extension registry — a map from module path to a substitution function, currently covering `ReactSharedInternals`, `ReactDOMSharedInternals`, `ReactFeatureFlags`, `SchedulerFeatureFlags`, `DefaultPrepareStackTrace`, `ReactFiberConfig`, `ReactServerStreamConfig`, `ReactFizzConfig`, `ReactFlightServerConfig`, `ReactFlightClientConfig`, `EventListener`, `useSyncExternalStore` and `isServerEnvironment`.

New runtime behaviour is introduced behind a flag in `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js`, mirrored into every fork under `packages/shared/forks/`, and surfaced to tests automatically as a `@gate` name by `TestFlags.js` (which requires `shared/ReactFeatureFlags` on demand).

The reconciler exposes a stable seam for schedulers: `ReactFiberRootScheduler.js#scheduleCallback` wraps `Scheduler_scheduleCallback(priorityLevel, callback)`, and the Scheduler itself is forked into `SchedulerMock`, `SchedulerNative`, `SchedulerPostTask` variants.

New compiler passes are inserted by editing the ordered pass list in `Entrypoint/Pipeline.ts` (and its Rust twin `entrypoint/pipeline.rs`); `compiler/CLAUDE.md` mandates reading `docs/passes/` for the pass being changed first.

Hook semantics are extensible through aliasing signatures registered in `src/HIR/Globals.ts` via `addHook(DEFAULT_SHAPES, {positionalParams, restParam, returnType, calleeEffect, hookKind, returnValueKind, aliasing: {receiver, params, rest, returns, temporaries, effects}}, id)` — missing an `aliasing` block silently falls back to `DefaultNonmutatingHook`.

Compiler feature flags are configured in `src/HIR/Environment.ts` and can be overridden per test fixture by a first-line comment pragma (e.g. `// enableJsxOutlining @enableNameAnonymousFunctions:false`).

The Rust crates are the extension surface for the port: eleven single-responsibility crates (`react_compiler_lowering`, `_ssa`, `_typeinference`, `_inference`, `_optimization`, `_reactive_scopes`, `_validation`, `_hir`, `_ast`, `_diagnostics`, `_utils`) wired through `Cargo.toml` workspace dependencies.

The ESLint plugin composes its rule table from two hand-written rules plus a spread of `allRules` from `shared/ReactCompiler`, and derives `recommended`/`recommendedLatest` presets by mapping compiler severities through `mapErrorSeverityToESlint` — new compiler diagnostics become lint rules without touching `index.ts`.

agent_handoff.summary: Treat `/compiler/` and everything else as two separate projects with separate package managers, lockfiles, CI workflows and conventions — the root `CLAUDE.md` says so explicitly, and `compiler/CLAUDE.md` even documents Sapling (`sl`) rather than git for that subtree. Never run `jest` or `rollup` directly; use `yarn test` / `yarn flow` / `yarn linc` / `yarn prettier`, and let CI do builds. The single most important structural fact to internalise before editing is the fork/shim system: `ReactFiberConfig`, `ReactFeatureFlags` and the flight/fizz configs resolve differently under Rollup, Jest and Flow, so 'it works in one channel' is not a signal. Read the work loop, the root scheduler and the feature-flag file before touching reconciler behaviour, and read the relevant `docs/passes/` doc before touching a compiler pass.

claims.claim: The repo is explicitly split: root `CLAUDE.md` scopes itself to 'All files outside `/compiler/`' and defers the compiler to its own instructions; `compiler/` has its own `package.json`, `yarn.lock`, `Cargo.toml` and CI workflows.

Read first, in order: `CLAUDE.md`, `packages/react-dom/src/client/ReactDOMRoot.js` (entry), `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` (the engine), `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberRootScheduler.js` (when work runs), `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js` (what's on), and `scripts/rollup/forks.js` + `scripts/shared/inlinedHostConfigs.js` (how modules actually resolve).

The prescribed pre-commit gate is `/verify`: `yarn prettier` → `yarn linc` (stop on failure), then `/flow`, `/test` and `/test www` in parallel — mirroring the CI jobs, so passing it locally is a strong predictor of green CI.
Yarn 1 is mandatory (`packageManager: yarn@1.22.22`) and Node is pinned by `.nvmrc`, which every CI job consumes via `node-version-file: '.nvmrc'`.

Do not invoke Jest directly — the root `jest.testRegex` deliberately points at `scripts/jest/dont-run-jest-directly.js`; run `yarn test -r <channel> --env <env>` instead, and `yarn test-www` / `yarn test-stable` for the common channels.

Do not build locally unless told to: root `CLAUDE.md` states 'Builds are handled by CI', and `yarn build` runs a multi-channel Rollup + Closure pipeline that also shells out to git and rewrites versions.
Adding a feature flag is a multi-file edit: the base `packages/shared/ReactFeatureFlags.js` plus each of the 13 forks under `packages/shared/forks/`, verified by `yarn flags` and the CI `flags` job.

Adding a user-visible `throw` requires running `yarn extract-errors` and committing the new entry in `scripts/error-codes/codes.json`; the script greps the `build` directory, so it only works after a build exists.
Tests that depend on a flag or channel must carry a `// @gate <expr>` pragma (supports `&&`, `!`, multiple gates); `FIXME`/`TODO` are reserved gate names that disable a test wholesale.

Compiler work has its own loop: `yarn snap` to run fixtures, `yarn snap -p <pattern> -d` to dump per-pass HIR, `yarn snap -u` to update `.expect.md`, `yarn snap compile <path>` for arbitrary files, `yarn snap minimize <path>` to shrink a repro.

Before implementing from a Rust-port plan doc, `compiler/CLAUDE.md` requires checking `git log --oneline --grep="<plan-name>"` and the plan's Remaining Work section; afterwards update the plan status, run `/compiler-verify`, and ensure `compiler/scripts/test-babel-ast.sh` passes.

Trap: `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberConfig.js` throws on import by design. If a new test or script resolves it, the fix is registering the renderer in `scripts/jest/setupHostConfigs.js` / `inlinedHostConfigs.js`, not editing the shim.

qaReadiness.summary: Repo does not expose enough local browser QA structure for a reliable Synthetic QA workflow yet.

readmePreview: This document serves as both a quick start guide to Redis and a detailed resource for building it from source.

overview.summary: This is the Redis Open Source server (`src/version.h` reports 8.9.241, branch `unstable`) — a single-process, event-loop-driven in-memory data structure server written in C99/gnu11, plus its CLI, benchmark, sentinel, and RDB/AOF checking tools. Beyond upstream Redis it carries a substantial in-tree feature layer: a new `OBJ_ARRAY` sparse-array type (`src/t_array.c`, `src/sparsearray.c`), key eviction protection (`src/bless.c`), CuckooHeavyKeeper hot-key tracking (`src/chk.c`, `src/hotkeys.c`), atomic cluster slot migration (`src/cluster_asm.c`), zstd replication/client compression (`src/client_comp.c`), and multi-threaded IO (`src/iothread.c`). It also ships a bespoke top-level Makefile + `scripts/` orchestration layer that clones, builds, deploys, and tests four external Redis modules (RediSearch, RedisJSON, RedisBloom, RedisTimeSeries) pinned by `modules/modules.yaml`, which upstream Redis does not have.

system_map.summary: The runtime is one `redis-server` binary whose `main()` in `src/server.c` initializes config, ACL, the module system and connection types, then hands control to the `ae` event loop (`aeMain`). The same binary multiplexes into sentinel, `redis-check-rdb` and `redis-check-aof` modes by argv[0] inspection. Storage is entirely in-process (`kvstore`/`dict`/`listpack`/`quicklist`/`rax`/`ebuckets`), persisted by RDB snapshot and/or AOF manifest, and replicated over a custom PSYNC protocol. Build is GNU Make: `src/Makefile` compiles the core and vendored `deps/`, while the top-level `Makefile` delegates to `scripts/*.sh` for the module-bundle workflow. Deployment shape is a bare binary + `redis.conf` (or the generated `redis-full.conf`), with an Ubuntu 24.04 build image in `docker/Dockerfile.noble`.

claims.claim: `main()` in src/server.c is the single entrypoint for redis-server, redis-sentinel, redis-check-rdb and redis-check-aof: it calls `checkForSentinelMode()` on argv, then dispatches to `redis_check_rdb_main()` / `redis_check_aof_main()` when `strstr(exec_name, "redis-check-rdb"/"redis-check-aof")` matches, before any config parsing.

Startup order in `main()` is fixed and dependency-driven: `initServerConfig()` → `ACLInit()` (commented 'must be initialized ASAP because the basic networking code and client creation depends on it') → `moduleInitModulesSystem()` → `connTypeInitialize()` → `keyMetaInit()`.

The event loop is created in `initServer()` via `aeCreateEventLoop(server.maxclients+CONFIG_FDSET_INCR)`, and per-DB storage is allocated as three parallel structures — `kvstoreCreate()` for `db->keys`, `db->expires`, plus `blessedKvstoreCreate()` for `db->blessed_keys` and `estoreCreate()` for `db->subexpires`.
`main()` ends with `aeMain(server.el)` after `redisSetCpuAffinity(server.server_cpulist)` and `setOOMScoreAdj(-1)`; everything after that point is event-loop driven.

The core links 130+ objects listed in `REDIS_SERVER_OBJ` in src/Makefile, including the non-upstream modules `bless.o t_array.o sparsearray.o chk.o hotkeys.o gcra.o vector.o fwtree.o estore.o client_comp.o cluster_asm.o iothread.o keymeta.o`.

Vendored third-party code lives in `deps/` and is built as separate targets: `DEPENDENCY_TARGETS=hiredis linenoise lua hdr_histogram fpconv xxhash tre` — note `tre` (regex) is a dependency of the new array type, which includes `../deps/tre/local_includes/tre.h`.

The top-level Makefile is not upstream's: it includes `modules/manifest.mk`, defines a `GOALS_WITH_ARGS` positional-argument capture mechanism, and routes `build`/`clean`/`test`/`deploy`/`bootstrap`/`run`/`tarball` to `scripts/*.sh` rather than recursing into `src/`.

`modules/modules.yaml` is the single source of truth pinning four external modules to immutable refs: redisbloom v8.11.81, redisearch v8.10.1 (with `build_env: LTO=1 REDISEARCH_GENERATE_HEADERS=0 INLINE_LSE_ATOMICS=0`), redisjson v8.10.0, redistimeseries v8.10.0.

Test entrypoints are four shell wrappers that locate tclsh 8.5–9.0 and invoke `tests/test_helper.tcl`: `./runtest`, `./runtest-moduleapi` (which first runs `$MAKE -C tests/modules` then names 48 `--single unit/moduleapi/*` suites), `./runtest-cluster`, `./runtest-sentinel`.

`make -C src test` depends on building redis-server, redis-check-aof, redis-cli, redis-benchmark and `module_tests` before shelling out to `(cd ..; ./runtest)`; `test-modules`, `test-sentinel`, `test-cluster` are separate targets.

External integrations are network protocols rather than SDKs: the cluster bus (`src/cluster_legacy.c`), the PSYNC replication protocol (`src/replication.c`), TLS via OpenSSL gated on `BUILD_TLS=yes|module` (`src/tls.c`), and optional zstd compression gated on `-DUSE_COMPRESSION=1` detected via pkg-config.

The deployment artifact set is defined by `scripts/deploy.sh` / `scripts/uninstall.sh`: core binaries and symlinks into `$(PREFIX)/bin` (default `/usr/local`) and module `.so` files into `$(PREFIX)/lib/redis/modules`, with `loadmodule` paths rewritten into a generated `redis-full.conf`.

feature_catalog.summary: User-facing surface is the RESP command set — 464 JSON command specs under `src/commands/` compiled into the 13k-line `src/commands.def`. Alongside the classic types (string/list/set/zset/hash/stream/HLL/geo/bitmap) this tree adds a first-class array type (AR* commands), key-blessing (BLESS), hot-key tracking (HOTKEYS), INCREX, hash-field expiration (HEXPIRE family), and a compiled-out GCRA rate limiter. Administrative surface spans ACL, CLIENT, CLUSTER (including atomic slot migration), CONFIG, FUNCTION, DEBUG, and the Sentinel command set. Client-side tooling ships as `redis-cli` (with a full cluster manager and ~60 flags), `redis-benchmark`, and the two check tools.

claims.claim: 464 command specification JSON files under `src/commands/` are the declarative source of the command table; `utils/generate-command-code.py` compiles them into `src/commands.def` (13,236 lines) via the `$(COMMANDS_DEF_FILENAME).def` Make rule.

A new `OBJ_ARRAY` (type 7) sparse-array data type is exposed via 18 commands — ARSET, ARGET, ARDEL, ARDELRANGE, ARGETRANGE, ARGREP, ARINFO, ARINSERT, ARLASTITEMS, ARLEN, ARMGET, ARMSET, ARNEXT, AROP, ARRING, ARSCAN, ARSEEK, ARCOUNT — implemented in `src/t_array.c` over `src/sparsearray.c`.

BLESS marks keys as never-evictable: the NO-EVICT bit lives in the kvBits byte after each kvobj, persists through RDB and AOF, and is exposed as BLESS SET/GET/CLEAR/SCAN plus an `blessed_keys` INFO counter backed by a per-DB `db->blessed_keys` index.

HOTKEYS START/STOP/GET/RESET/HELP expose a CuckooHeavyKeeper top-K sketch (`src/chk.c`, based on the Ngo & Papatriantafilou paper plus a min-heap borrowed from RedisBloom's TopK) that can be scoped to specific cluster slot ranges via a `slotRangeArray`.
INCREX is a new string command returning a two-element reply (`{value, applied}`) that creates a missing key at 0 before incrementing, with an optional increment argument.

Hash-field expiration ships as eight commands — HEXPIRE, HEXPIREAT, HPEXPIRE, HPEXPIREAT, HEXPIRETIME, HPEXPIRETIME, HGETEX, HGETDEL — backed by the `ebuckets` radix-of-buckets expiry structure and the per-DB `estore` subexpires store.

A GCRA (Generic Cell Rate Algorithm) leaky-bucket rate limiter exists as `src/gcra.c` with an `OBJ_GCRA` object type and a 4-arg `GCRA key max_burst tokens_per_period period` command, ported from redis-cell — but it is compiled out by default behind `#ifdef ENABLE_GCRA`.

Atomic slot migration is a user-facing cluster feature driven by `CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT <slots>` run on the destination node, handled by `clusterMigrationCommand()`, with an eight-step protocol documented in the file header.

Lua scripting is offered in two forms: ephemeral EVAL/EVALSHA/SCRIPT via `evalGenericCommand()` and `luaCreateFunction()` in `src/eval.c`, and persistent FUNCTION libraries via a pluggable engine registry in `src/functions.c` whose only registered engine is `LUA_ENGINE_NAME` from `src/function_lua.c`.

`redis-cli` is a large multi-mode tool (11,561 lines) exposing analysis modes `--bigkeys --memkeys --hotkeys --keystats-samples --scan --latency --latency-dist --latency-history --intrinsic-latency --lru-test --rdb --functions-rdb --pipe --replica --eval --ldb`, RESP3/JSON output modes, and TLS flags (`--tls --cert --key --cacert --cacertdir --insecure`).

`redis-cli --cluster` embeds a full cluster manager dispatch table of `clusterManagerCommandProc` functions — create, add-node, del-node, info, check, fix, reshard, rebalance — with ~25 `--cluster-*` option flags.

Sentinel is a distinct operating mode of the same binary: `initSentinelConfig()` + `initSentinel()` run before config parsing so the config file populates monitored-master state, and `sentinelIsRunning()` replaces the normal ready-to-serve path in `main()`.

data_flow.summary: Input arrives on a connection abstraction (`connection.h` over socket/unix/TLS), is read into a per-client or thread-reusable query buffer by `readQueryFromClient()`, parsed into `pendingCommand` structs by `processInlineBuffer()`/`processMultibulkBuffer()`, dispatched by `processCommand()` and executed by `call()`. Command handlers mutate the authoritative state owner — `server.db[j]` kvstores — and any side effects are queued through `alsoPropagate()`. At the end of the execution unit `propagateNow()` fans out to exactly three sinks: the AOF buffer, the replica stream, and the atomic-slot-migration client. Replies accumulate in per-client output buffers and are flushed in `beforeSleep()` by `handleClientsWithPendingWrites()`, strictly after `flushAppendOnlyFile()` so `appendfsync=always` is honoured before acknowledgement.

claims.claim: The input boundary is `readQueryFromClient(connection *conn)`, which recovers the client via `connGetPrivateData(conn)` and reads `PROTO_IOBUF_LEN` bytes, except when a multibulk argument exceeds `PROTO_MBULK_BIG_ARG`, in which case it sizes the read to exactly the remaining bulk length to enable zero-copy object creation.

Query buffers are pooled per IO thread: a client with no private `querybuf` borrows `thread_reusable_qb` and sets `CLIENT_IO_REUSABLE_QUERYBUFFER`; if `thread_reusable_qb_used` is already set (nested execution via `processEventsWhileBlocked()`) the client allocates a private buffer instead.

`processInputBuffer()` parses ahead up to `server.lookahead` commands into `c->pending_cmds`, but clamps the lookahead to 1 for unauthenticated clients because AUTH changes the handling of succeeding commands.

Request type is inferred from the first byte: `'*'` selects `PROTO_REQ_MULTIBULK` → `processMultibulkBuffer()`, anything else selects `PROTO_REQ_INLINE` → `processInlineBuffer()`; an unknown `reqtype` triggers `serverPanic("Unknown request type")`.

`processCommand()` resolves argv to a `struct redisCommand` through a three-tier lookup: an already-set `c->lookedcmd`, then `isCommandReusable(c->lastcmd, ...)` reusing the previous command, then a full `lookupCommand(c->argv, c->argc)`.

The command table itself is populated once at startup by `populateCommandTable()` walking the generated `extern struct redisCommand redisCommandTable[]` from commands.def, so adding a command is a data change in `src/commands/*.json` followed by codegen.

Module command filters get first look at every non-reprocessed command: `processCommand()` calls `moduleCallCommandFilters(c)` and `reqresAppendRequest(c)` before command lookup, meaning a module can rewrite argv before the core ever resolves the command name.

`call()` records `dirty = server.dirty` and `old_master_repl_offset = server.master_repl_offset` before invoking the proc, and clears `CLIENT_FORCE_AOF|CLIENT_FORCE_REPL|CLIENT_PREVENT_PROP` so the handler must opt back into propagation.

`server.allowed_propagate_targets` is a global mask narrowed for the duration of each `call()` so that nested `RM_Call`/Lua `redis.set_repl()` restrictions from an outer call cannot be escaped by an inner one — this is what makes effect-command rewriting (SPOP→SREM) honour selective replication.

`propagateNow()` is the single fan-out point to the three output sinks: `feedAppendOnlyFile()` when `server.aof_state != AOF_OFF && target & PROPAGATE_AOF`, then `replicationFeedSlaves(server.slaves, ...)` and `asmFeedMigrationClient(argv, argc)` when `target & PROPAGATE_REPL`.

`propagateNow()` asserts that propagation never happens while replica actions are paused — `serverAssert(!(isPausedActions(PAUSE_ACTION_REPLICA) && !server.client_pause_in_transaction))` — because a dataset change during a replica pause could be lost on failover.

Output ordering in `beforeSleep()` is load-bearing and commented as such: `connTypeProcessPendingData()` and `clientCompressionProcessPendingData()` must run before `flushAppendOnlyFile(0)`, which must run before `handleClientsWithPendingWrites()` and `sendPendingClientsToIOThreads()` so `appendfsync=always` is satisfied before the reply is sent.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows dominate. Startup: `main()` → config → subsystem init → `initServer()` → `InitServerLast()` → `loadDataFromDisk()` → AOF reconciliation → `aeMain()`. Command execution: socket readable → `readQueryFromClient()` → `processInputBuffer()` → `processCommandAndResetClient()` → `processCommand()` → `call()` → handler → `alsoPropagate()` → `propagatePendingCommands()` → `propagateNow()`. Replica bootstrap: `replicaofCommand()` → `replicationSetMaster()` → `connectWithMaster()` → `syncWithMaster()` handshake → `slaveTryPartialResynchronization()` → full sync via `readSyncBulkPayload()`, with the master side running `syncCommand()` → `startBgsaveForReplication()` → `rdbSaveToSlavesSockets()`.

claims.claim: STARTUP step 1 — `main()` seeds entropy from `time(NULL)^getpid()^tv.tv_usec` into `srand`/`srandom`/`init_genrand64`, calls `crc64_init()`, captures `umask(server.umask = umask(0777))` early to avoid a thread race, and seeds the dict hash with 16 bytes from `getRandomBytes()` — this is what makes hash-flooding attacks impractical.

STARTUP step 2 — argv parsing in `main()` conceptually appends every `--opt value` pair onto the config file text as newline-separated directives, with documented precedence 'File, stdin, explicit options -- last config is the one that matters', plus special-cases for bare `--save` and `--sentinel`.

STARTUP step 3 — `initServer()` installs `SIG_IGN` for SIGHUP/SIGPIPE, runs `setupSignalHandlers()`, `ThreadsManager_init()`, `makeThreadKillable()`, then `hashTemplatesInit()`, `createSharedObjects()`, `adjustOpenFilesLimit()` and `monotonicInit(monotonicLogCallback)` before creating the event loop.

STARTUP step 4 — `initServer()` decides memory accounting once and irreversibly: `server.memory_tracking_enabled = server.key_memory_histograms || clusterSlotStatsEnabled(CLUSTER_SLOT_STATS_MEM)`, documented as disable-able at runtime but never re-enable-able to avoid a full slot re-scan.

STARTUP step 5 — `InitServerLast()` starts the background subsystems last: `bioInit()`, `initThreadedIO()`, `set_jemalloc_bg_thread()`, and records `server.initial_memory_usage = zmalloc_used_memory()` as the baseline for memory reporting.

STARTUP step 6 — the load sequence in `main()` is `aofLoadManifestFromDisk()` → `loadDataFromDisk()` → `aofSetupAfterPreloadFile()` → `aofOpenIfNeededOnServerStart()` → `aofDelHistoryFiles()` → `applyAppendOnlyConfig()`, the last of which exists specifically to apply an `appendonly` config change that arrived while loading.

STARTUP step 7 — in cluster mode `main()` hard-asserts `verifyClusterConfigWithData() == C_OK` after load, then logs 'Ready to accept connections' per non-NULL `server.listeners[j]`, notifies systemd with `READY=1` when `supervised_mode == SUPERVISED_SYSTEMD`, and finally calls `warnAboutInsecureConfig()`.

COMMAND step 1 — `processCommand()` first postpones the client via `blockPostponeClient(c)` if a module is in a blocked yield that excludes `BUSY_MODULE_YIELD_CLIENTS`, then runs `commandCheckExistence()` and `commandCheckArity()`, rejecting via `rejectCommandSds()`.

COMMAND step 2 — commands literally named `host:` or `post` are intercepted before any other handling and routed to `securityWarningCommand(c)` returning `C_ERR`, a cross-protocol-scripting (HTTP-to-Redis) defence.

COMMAND step 3 — commands carrying `CMD_INTERNAL` are made to look nonexistent (`cmd = NULL`) unless the client has `CLIENT_INTERNAL` or `mustObeyClient(c)` is true, so masters and AOF replay are implicitly trusted while ordinary clients cannot even discover them.

COMMAND step 4 — `CMD_PROTECTED` commands are gated by `allowProtectedAction(server.enable_debug_cmd, c)` for `debugCommand` and `server.enable_module_cmd` for `moduleCommand`, with an error naming `enable-debug-command`/`enable-module-command`.

COMMAND step 5 — `call()` sets `CLIENT_EXECUTING_COMMAND` to suppress mid-reply client-side-caching pushes, calls `enterExecutionUnit(1, call_timer)`, and skips slowlog/stat updates entirely when `isAOFLoadingContext()` is true.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is a Tcl integration suite: `tests/test_helper.tcl` globs `tests/{unit,unit/type,unit/moduleapi,unit/cluster,integration}/*.tcl` into `::all_tests` and runs them against real spawned `redis-server` processes on ports from 21111. There are no C-level unit test files, but the binary embeds a `REDIS_TEST` mode invoked as `redis-server test <name>|all` for data-structure self-tests. Module API coverage is unusually deep — 48 C test modules under `tests/modules/` paired with 48 `unit/moduleapi/*.tcl` suites. CI runs eight build matrices plus an ASAN build and a commands.def drift check, with lcov/Codecov, CodeQL, Coverity, and a reply-schema linter on separate workflows.

claims.claim: Test discovery is directory-glob based, not a manifest: `test_helper.tcl` iterates `set test_dirs {unit unit/type unit/moduleapi unit/cluster integration}` and lsorts `*.tcl` into `::all_tests`, so a new `.tcl` file in those dirs is picked up automatically.

The harness is a client/server fan-out: `test_server_main`, `accept_test_clients`, `read_from_test_client` and `signal_idle_client` distribute test files across parallel Tcl clients, with `run_solo` for tests that must not run concurrently.

Support libraries sourced by every suite live in `tests/support/`: `server.tcl` (start_server), `util.tcl`, `cluster_util.tcl`, `aofmanifest.tcl`, `redis.tcl` (the Tcl RESP client), `response_transformers.tcl` (RESP2/RESP3 normalisation), and `cli.tcl`.

Module API is the most thoroughly covered subsystem: `runtest-moduleapi` enumerates 48 suites explicitly by `--single`, and `tests/modules/` holds 48 matching C test modules built by `$MAKE -C tests/modules` before the run.

The C code carries an embedded self-test harness rather than a separate unit-test binary: `main()` under `#ifdef REDIS_TEST` accepts `redis-server test <name>|all` with flags `--accurate --large-memory --valgrind --verbose`, iterates a `redisTests[]` table, and prints a pass/fail summary.

Cluster coverage includes 23 dedicated suites under `tests/unit/cluster/`, notably `atomic-slot-migration.tcl`, `internal-secret.tcl`, `packet-validation.tcl`, `tls-peer-impersonation.tcl` and `cluster-bus-port-protected-mode.tcl` — the security-sensitive cluster paths are explicitly exercised.

Integration coverage focuses on durability and replication edge cases: `aof-multi-part.tcl`, `aof-race.tcl`, `corrupt-dump-fuzzer.tcl`, `corrupt-dump.tcl`, `psync2*.tcl` (four files), `replication-rdbchannel.tcl`, `replication-iothreads.tcl`, `failover.tcl`, `shutdown.tcl`.
The primary CI job `test-ubuntu-latest` builds with `make REDIS_CFLAGS='-Werror' BUILD_TLS=yes` and runs `./runtest --verbose --tags -slow --dump-logs` — meaning slow-tagged tests do not gate PRs.

CI enforces codegen freshness: the `validate commands.def up to date` step touches `src/commands/ping.json`, runs `make commands.def`, and fails if `git diff` is non-empty — a hand-edited commands.def will break the build.

A dedicated `test-sanitizer-address` job builds `SANITIZER=address REDIS_CFLAGS='-Werror -DDEBUG_ASSERTIONS -DREDIS_TEST' BUILD_TLS=module` and reruns the suite, so debug assertions and the embedded C tests are compiled in on that path only.

The build matrix covers portability rather than behaviour: `build-debian-old` (debian:buster container), `build-macos-latest`, `build-32bit` (via gcc-multilib), `build-libc-malloc`, `build-centos-jemalloc` (centos:stream9) and `build-old-chain-jemalloc` — all compile-only, no test step.

Coverage is reported but non-gating: `codecov.yml` sets both `patch` and `project` statuses to `informational: true`, and the workflow runs `make lcov` and uploads `./src/redis.info`, gated on `github.repository == 'redis/redis'` so forks skip it.

risk_map.summary: The dominant risk class is memory-safety in hand-written C parsing code reachable pre-authentication: the RESP parser, the cluster bus packet decoder, and the RDB/DUMP loader all consume untrusted bytes. Authentication is layered and easy to misconfigure — protected-mode, ACL, an auto-generated cluster internal secret, and module-supplied auth callbacks. A second class is coupling risk: the propagation invariants in `call()`/`propagateNow()`, the ordering contract inside `beforeSleep()`, and the object-type registration checklist all fail silently or assert if a contributor misses a step. Finally, there is genuinely dead code — GCRA is compiled out and its test file is `if 0`'d — and a large `DEBUG` surface with 50+ subcommands guarded only by a config flag.

claims.claim: The RESP parser is the pre-auth attack surface: `processMultibulkBuffer()` and `processInlineBuffer()` parse attacker-controlled bytes into `pendingCommand` structs before any AUTH check, and `readQueryFromClient()` performs manual pointer arithmetic (`(size_t)(c->bulklen+2)-(sdslen(c->querybuf)-c->qb_pos)`) to size big-argument reads.

The cluster internal secret is auto-generated with `getRandomHexChars(server.cluster->internal_secret, CLUSTER_INTERNALSECRETLEN)` and converged across nodes by a lexicographic `memcmp(...) > 0` rule in the PING extension handler — meaning any node that can join the bus can influence the shared secret used to authenticate internal connections.

Internal-secret password comparison correctly uses `time_independent_strcmp()`, but it is one of several parallel auth paths (`checkPasswordBasedAuth`, `ACLAuthenticateUser`, module auth callbacks) that must all stay consistent — a change to one does not automatically cover the others.

`moduleLoad()` calls `dlopen(path, RTLD_NOW|RTLD_LOCAL)` on an operator-supplied path, giving any successfully loaded module full in-process code execution; the only guard is that `MODULE` carries `CMD_PROTECTED` and is gated by `server.enable_module_cmd`.
`warnAboutInsecureConfig()` only logs — it never refuses to start. A server with `DefaultUser` NOPASS, `protected-mode no` and a `0.0.0.0`/`::` bind emits a WARNING and then serves traffic.

`redis-server --test-memory <mb>` and `--check-system` run arbitrary memory-stressing code (`memtest()`, `syscheck()`) directly from `main()` before any config or privilege handling, and `--test-memory` with a non-numeric argument silently becomes `atoi(...) == 0`.

`src/debug.c` dispatches roughly 52 `DEBUG` subcommands via a chain of `strcasecmp(c->argv[1]->ptr, ...)` comparisons; the entire surface is protected only by the `enable-debug-command` config and `allowProtectedAction()`, and several subcommands (JMAP, SEGFAULT, SET-ACTIVE-EXPIRE, QUICKLIST-PACKED-THRESHOLD) can corrupt or crash a live server.

Adding a new object type is a documented multi-file checklist with no compiler enforcement — the `server.h` comment requires coordinated edits to `rdb.c` (save/load, possibly RDB_VERSION), `aof.c` (rewrite), `db.c` (`obj_type_name`, `copyCommand`), `debug.c` (`xorObjectDigest`, `serverLogObjectDebugInfo`) and `defrag.c` (`defragKey`). Missing one produces silent data or defrag corruption, not a build error.

GCRA is dead code in the shipped build: `src/gcra.c` is entirely inside `#ifdef ENABLE_GCRA`, `OBJ_GCRA`/`OBJ_TYPE_MAX 9` are conditional in `server.h`, the guard appears in `rdb.h`, `redismodule.h` and `acl.c`, and `tests/unit/gcra.tcl` disables its whole body with `if 0 {`. Building with `-DENABLE_GCRA` would activate untested code and change `OBJ_TYPE_MAX`, which is an RDB-visible constant.

`beforeSleep()` encodes at least four ordering invariants in comments rather than in code structure (TLS pending data before AOF flush; `clusterBeforeSleep()` before `blockedBeforeSleep()`; `blockedBeforeSleep()` before `flushAppendOnlyFile`; AOF flush before `handleClientsWithPendingWrites`). Reordering any of them breaks `appendfsync=always` durability guarantees without failing a test deterministically.

`propagateNow()` contains two assertions that convert logic errors into crashes rather than data loss: `debugServerAssert(duration != PROP_DURATION_UNKNOWN)` and the replica-pause assert. Both are reachable from any new command that queues propagation incorrectly.

The query-buffer pooling scheme (`thread_reusable_qb` / `thread_reusable_qb_used` / `CLIENT_IO_REUSABLE_QUERYBUFFER`) is shared mutable state whose correctness depends on nested-execution detection; the code comment notes the private-buffer fallback exists only for `processEventsWhileBlocked()` re-entry.

extension_points.summary: Redis has four first-class extension mechanisms. New commands are added declaratively: drop a JSON spec in `src/commands/`, implement the proc, and regenerate `src/commands.def`. New configuration parameters are appended to the `static_configs[]` table in `src/config.c` using the `create*Config` macro family. New runtime behaviour is added out-of-process via the module API (`RM_CreateCommand`/`RM_CreateSubcommand` plus data types, filters, and hooks). New scripting languages plug into `functionsRegisterEngine()`. On top of these, this tree adds a fifth: `modules/modules.yaml` as a declarative registry for bundled external modules.

claims.claim: Command registration is codegen-driven: `src/commands/*.json` is the input, `utils/generate-command-code.py` is the generator, and `src/Makefile`'s rule `$(COMMANDS_DEF_FILENAME).def: commands/*.json ../utils/generate-command-code.py` regenerates `src/commands.def`. CI fails if the checked-in file drifts.

The generator maps declarative JSON to C enums via `ARG_TYPES` (string/integer/double/key/pattern/unix-time/pure-token/oneof/block) and `GROUPS`, which already contains the newer `COMMAND_GROUP_ARRAY` and `COMMAND_GROUP_RATE_LIMIT` — adding a command group means editing this table.

The runtime command registry is `redisCommandTable[]` from commands.def, loaded once by `populateCommandTable()` into dicts consulted by `lookupCommandLogic()`, `lookupCommandBySds()` and `lookupCommandByCString()` — module commands are inserted into the same dicts.

Configuration is a single append-only table: `standardConfig static_configs[]` in src/config.c, populated by 119 `createBoolConfig`/`createStringConfig`/`createEnumConfig`/`createSDSConfig`/etc. calls, each taking a flags mask (`MODIFIABLE_CONFIG`, `IMMUTABLE_CONFIG`, `DEBUG_CONFIG`, `HIDDEN_CONFIG`, `SENSITIVE_CONFIG`) plus optional validate and apply callbacks.

Config apply-callbacks are the hook for cross-subsystem side effects — e.g. `updateClusterFlags` on `cluster-replica-no-failover`, `updateJemallocBgThread` on `jemalloc-bg-thread`, `updateAppendonly` on `appendonly`, `updateRequirePass` on `requirepass`, and `applyClusterBusPortProtectedMode`.

The module command API is `RM_CreateCommand(ctx, name, cmdfunc, strflags, firstkey, lastkey, keystep)` with `RM_CreateSubcommand(parent, ...)` for containers — the canonical way third-party code adds commands without touching the core tables.

Modules can intercept every command before dispatch by registering a command filter, invoked as `moduleCallCommandFilters(c)` at the top of `processCommand()`; `src/module.c` documents a flag to prevent a module's own `RM_Call()` from re-entering its filter.

Server lifecycle hooks are exposed as module server events — `beforeSleep()` fires `moduleFireServerEvent(REDISMODULE_EVENT_EVENTLOOP, REDISMODULE_SUBEVENT_EVENTLOOP_BEFORE_SLEEP, NULL)` once per loop iteration when `moduleCount()` is non-zero.

Scripting languages are pluggable through `functionsRegisterEngine(const char *engine_name, engine *engine)`, which stores into a module-level `static dict *engines`; `FUNCTION STATS` reflects the registry back to clients, and the only current registration is `LUA_ENGINE_NAME` from `luaEngineInitEngine` in function_lua.c.

Keyspace notification is a central hook point via `notifyKeyspaceEvent(type, event, key, dbid)` and the newer `notifyKeyspaceEventWithSubkeys(...)` — new data types must call these to participate in keyspace events and client-side-cache invalidation.

Connection types are a runtime-registered abstraction: `connTypeInitialize()` in `main()` sets up `server.listeners[j]` for `j < CONN_TYPE_MAX`, with implementations in `src/socket.c`, `src/unix.c` and `src/tls.c` behind `src/connection.h` — TLS can even be built as a loadable module with `BUILD_TLS=module`.

Bundled external modules are added declaratively by appending an entry to `modules/modules.yaml` with `name`/`repo`/`ref`/`target_module`/`loadmodule` and optional `build_env` — no new Makefile is needed, because `modules/common.mk` derives `MODULE_NAME` from `$(notdir $(CURDIR))` and reads the rest from the manifest.

agent_handoff.summary: Read `src/server.h` (the 4,976-line master header that every `.c` file includes) and `src/server.c` before touching anything — nearly all global state hangs off the `server` struct declared there. Never hand-edit `src/commands.def`; edit the JSON spec and regenerate. Prefer adding config via the `static_configs[]` table and features via the module API over touching the dispatch path. Build with `make REDIS_CFLAGS='-Werror'` to match CI, and validate with `./runtest --tags -slow` plus `./runtest-moduleapi` if you touched `src/module.c`. Be aware this tree's root `Makefile` is not upstream's: plain `make` runs `scripts/build.sh`, which builds `src/` and then every cloned external module.

claims.claim: Read first, in order: `src/server.h` (all struct/constant/prototype definitions), `src/server.c` (`main`, `initServer`, `processCommand`, `call`, `beforeSleep`, `serverCron`), `src/networking.c` (client lifecycle and RESP parsing), and `src/config.c` (`static_configs[]`).

Never edit `src/commands.def` by hand. Edit `src/commands/<cmd>.json`, run `make commands.def` (which invokes `utils/generate-command-code.py`), and commit both — CI's `validate commands.def up to date` step diffs the regenerated output and fails on drift.

Match CI's build flags locally: `make REDIS_CFLAGS='-Werror' BUILD_TLS=yes`. Use `REDIS_CFLAGS`/`REDIS_LDFLAGS` rather than `CFLAGS`/`LDFLAGS` — the src/Makefile header notes that plain CFLAGS propagate into the `deps/` builds (jemalloc, Lua, hiredis) too.

Test commands to run: `make -C src test` (= `./runtest`) for the default suite, `./runtest --tags -slow --dump-logs` to match CI exactly, `./runtest --single unit/type/hash` to scope, `make -C src test-modules`, `test-cluster`, `test-sentinel` for the other three harnesses.

Trap — building Redis alone is `make -C src all`, not `make`. The root `Makefile`'s default goal is `build`, which runs `scripts/build.sh` and will additionally try to build every module cloned under `modules/*/src`. Use `make build redis` or `make build core` to skip modules.

Trap — on macOS you must use `gmake` (GNU Make ≥ 4.x), not Apple's `/usr/bin/make` 3.81. The root Makefile explicitly `export MAKE`s so recipe shells inherit the right binary, precisely because non-interactive recipe shells otherwise PATH-resolve to make 3.81.

Trap — adding a new object type requires coordinated edits to `rdb.c`, `aof.c`, `db.c` (`obj_type_name`, `copyCommand`), `debug.c` (`xorObjectDigest`, `serverLogObjectDebugInfo`) and `defrag.c` (`defragKey`), per the checklist comment in server.h. Nothing enforces this at compile time.

Trap — `redis.conf` is the tracked, hand-edited core config with no markers; `redis-full.conf` is untracked and regenerated by `scripts/sync-redis-conf.sh` on every `make modules-update`. Never hand-add `loadmodule` lines to `redis.conf`.

Safe edit boundary — prefer adding behaviour through the module API (`RM_CreateCommand`, module data types, command filters, server-event hooks) or a new `static_configs[]` entry over modifying `processCommand()`/`call()`, which carry assertions and propagation invariants.

Do not touch `deps/` — it is vendored third-party source (jemalloc, lua, hiredis, linenoise, hdr_histogram, fpconv, xxhash, tre) built by separate targets listed in `DEPENDENCY_TARGETS`. Changes there are lost on dependency refresh.

Style convention — the codebase is C99/gnu11 compiled with `-pedantic -Wall -W -Wstrict-prototypes -Werror=deprecated-declarations`, and falls back to `-std=c99` (also setting `SKIP_VEC_SETS=yes`) when the compiler lacks C11 `_Atomic`. New code must build under both.

Licensing convention — every new source file carries the Redis tri-license header (RSALv2 / SSPLv1 / AGPLv3); contributions are governed by the Software Grant and CLA reproduced in full in CONTRIBUTING.md.
